Recently, 6DoF pose estimation from monocular images has gained significant interest.
This task is challenging due to its high dimensionalality and variability in object appearance.
To tackle this issue, researchers have successfully applied neural networks to pose estimation tasks.
However, these methods typically focus on predicting pose coordinates without consideration for the object's layout, leading to lower than desired performance.
To enhance pose estimation results, researchers have used neural networks to forecast the 2D layout of objects from images.
In this work, we integrate 2D object layout prediction with clustering and neural network-based correspondence learning to determine the 6DoF pose.
Specific projection maps are derived from the trained network for easy access, simplifying the process of finding a pose that corresponds to the underlying scene structure.
We demonstrated that this method's performance is superior to other baselines in experiments conducted on the SUN3D and AIR dataset.
In addition, we show that removing the network's ability to learn correspondences results in a method similar to traditional re-projection based evaluation, and that this method's ability to generalize is comparable to other neural network-based pose estimation methods despite its simple structure. 
This approach's potential for use in other tasks such as object detection and segmentation also becomes apparent in this work. 
We made public the code and model for this project.

This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we establish a direct relationship between the coefficients of the complex self-dual electromagnetic field and the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the Newman-Penrose formalism. Additionally, it enables the construction of a specific type of polynomial, termed an odd-square polynomial, which can be advantageous in various programming applications. A key feature of this technique is that it avoids the utilization of well-known and frequently utilized mathematical principles, such as the modulus operator, the absolute value function, and the concept of congruence. As a result, this method can be employed across a broad spectrum of programming frameworks, including but not limited to Erlang, Prolog, and ML, by treating these frameworks as if they were abstract rings. This framework involves selecting a particular property of the ring theory and deriving the beneficial property of the odd-square polynomials, along with demonstrating how this benefits the programming task at hand. A novel medical image segmentation technique called Dense Focus Unet (DFU) has been previously introduced to efficiently process large images. This framework incorporates a spatially reduced patch-based approach for efficient data processing and applies the principle of U-net for feature extraction. Building on this foundation, a modified DFU called DDAUnet was developed to better suit esophageal CT scan data by incorporating atrium density as an additional input feature and implementing a focal technique to address class imbalance. DDAUnet was applied to esophageal neoplasm segmentation with outstanding results, achieving a high Dice coefficient of 0.78, outperforming existing methods in the esophageal neoplasm segmentation challenge. This technique's effectiveness was also demonstrated across various data set combinations, further highlighting its efficacy. Human-generated descriptions serve a purpose beyond simple data augmentation; they can be used to train and evaluate language models for automatic image descriptions. This paper discusses methods that researchers can use to incorporate human descriptions into training models, as well as techniques for evaluating them. We also present a simplified framework consisting of two primary assessments: a human-only section where subjects compare automatic descriptions to human-generated ones, and a mixed-human section where subjects select preferred descriptions from a mix of human and automatic descriptions. This framework can be used for various evaluation settings and provides detailed data to support methodological discussions. Our objective is to contribute a straightforward, easily implementable framework that other researchers can build upon. Our code is available online at https://github.com/alevy/Description-Evaluation. We invite other researchers to try this framework, suggest improvements, and provide alternate methods of evaluating automatic image descriptions. Our primary area of interest is in describing and evaluating the effectiveness of various automatic image description generation models, particularly the simple recursive neural network introduced by Vinyals et al. in 2015. Our framework has been applied to this NNN model, which is a two-layer model, as well as a more complex state-of-the-art model, the advanced neural tiled attention model introduced by Guo et al. in 2019. We believe that evaluating automatic image description generation models is crucial; it can be achieved by comparing the human-generated and automatic descriptions using a relative ranking method that accounts for the diversity of descriptions, in addition to their similarity. Our evaluation tool consists of a simple, scalable design that can be used to evaluate models on a small group of images prior to deploying them on larger datasets. Our results show that the NNN model produces more accurate descriptions than the tiled neural network model, while the tiled neural network model prioritizes brevity over accuracy. Our analysis indicates that the primary limitation of the NNN model is its lack of diversity, in addition to its difficulty in generating concise descriptions. Our framework provides a straightforward method of evaluating the quality of automatic image description generation models, as demonstrated by our results, which also show that the NNN model produces high-quality descriptions on a large dataset. Our code consists of a Python script that uses the Description Evaluation Tool to generate the data and the human comparison interface, in addition to a Google Colab notebook that provides an interactive version of the tool. Our future work involves developing a more sophisticated comparison method, as well as a system for automatically generating descriptions based on human feedback. Tantalum oxide compounds, with their versatile properties, have gained significant attention for electronic applications. To further develop this material, understanding its fundamental property, the spontaneous polarization, relies on accurately determining the crystal structure of a specific compound, Ta$_2$O$_5$. However, identifying its structure is challenging due to the presence of multiple possible configurations and phases of the material. We investigated Ta$_2$O$_5$'s structure in its ground state, examining different configurations and phases, and have determined the most stable state of Ta$_2$O$_5$. We found that a particular configuration, based on experimental data, is the ground state of Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically the polymorph Ta$_2$O$_5$ (B) with a tetragonal crystal structure. We also verified our results by comparing our ab initio and Monte Carlo simulation findings. Lastly, we discussed the unique property of spontaneous polarization in Ta$_2$O$_5$ (B), indicating that it could be influenced by external electric field effects. Moreover, we examined the phases and structures of Ta$_2$O$_5$ using a $\Gamma$-K$\Gamma$ path in reciprocal space, and have made a supposition about the behavior of this material in bulk form. Lastly, we discussed the possible relationships between Ta$_2$O$_5$'s different phases, and the conditions required to stabilize the ground state configuration, concluding that researching this further is crucial.

This research investigates the prevalence and dissemination patterns of false information on the Big Geographic Arrangement (EGA) among Reddit users in the United States. To achieve this, a false information detection method was developed and applied to a dataset of claims made on Reddit forums from 2015 to 2020. The analysis identified 1,699 false claims related to categories such as politics, health, science and technology, history and culture, and economics and environment. A propagation analysis of these claims among Reddit users revealed the EGA transmission structure. The study found that false information propagates rapidly across the A-layer and the C-layer, but is hindered in the B-layer. The results also indicate that the key factor limiting the spread of false information is not the B-layer's moderate population size, but rather the impenetrable barriers it presents, creating geographic arrangements that minimize the exchange with adjacent B-layer regions. The analysis further discovered that the main obstacles to the spread of false information are not the B-layer's population size or the distance between regions, but rather the lack of connectivity between areas and the limited scope for global propagation. The research highlights the significance of the Big Geographic Arrangement in controlling the dissemination of false information and highlights the importance of understanding the complex dynamics of knowledge networks in the digital age. The study's false information detection method and propagation analysis of the EGA transmission structure also provide a foundation for exploring similar patterns in other contexts. The appendices include a detailed explanation of the false information detection method used in this study. Humans follow instructions from others to accomplish various tasks, and understanding how they process auditory instructions is crucial for enhancing robot performance. Although previous research primarily focused on how to provide clear audio directions to robots, it neglected analysis of how human instructors structure their instructions. This study examines how humans deliver audio instructions for robot activities by exploring the relationship between their verbal descriptions and corresponding robot manipulations. A novel method was developed to analyze the temporal relationship between audio instructions and robot movements. Utilizing this approach, a group of participants was instructed to convey different activities to a robot via audio, and their speech was correlated with the robot's movements. The outcome revealed that humans generally describe a movement before executing it, although this pattern varies depending on the activity type. Interestingly, a difference was observed in instruction delivery depending on whether the activity involves a single action or a sequence of actions. The findings have implications for developing more effective audio commands that enhance robot performance by considering the temporal structure of human instructions. Moreover, this research can be applied to various domains, including but not limited to, teaching robots via demonstration. Ultimately, understanding human instruction patterns will contribute to creating a learning platform that enables robots to learn from human demonstrations and generalizes across different activities. The study's results are available online for further exploration. The data underlying this research may be used as a starting point for developing a system that generates instructions from demonstrated activities, as well as providing a valuable resource for researchers working on various aspects of human robot interaction. Conversational interfaces such as voice assistants like Amazon Alexa and virtual chatbots have become increasingly popular, and their development costs are continually rising. To manage the growth, a automated assessment method is necessary to evaluate conversational bots quickly and efficiently. Despite the demand for such a method, developing conversational interfaces is still largely a manual process. In this paper, we present an automated assessment framework for conversational bots in English, focusing on their user interface. We also discuss the method's applicability to user interface designs and conversational dialogue management systems. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target scenarios are commonly explored; however, research on multi-sparse-domain cooperation is less frequent and may offer the most substantial benefits. Existing methods often incorporate static domain classifications or rely on heuristic parameters, which can result in suboptimal performance. Additionally, by directly combining domain-specific preferences without consideration of user-domain interactions, they may run the risk of overwhelming the system with diverse domain preferences. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperation via Aspect Preference Learning (MSDCA) framework that dynamically determines user-domain attachments based on user-feature interactions, and a subsequent improved thorough aspect preference learning process that incorporates a contrastive non-negative mean square error mechanism to enhance the effectiveness of adapting to diverse domains. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets showcase the MSDCA framework's superiority over existing methods in multiple scenarios. The MSDCA framework is suited for multi-sparse-domain cooperation and has the potential to extract valuable insights for general cross-domain recommendation scenarios. The associated code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang0606/Multi-Sparse-Domain-Cooperation.

Conic programming is a highly effective method for solving a wide range of difficult optimization problems, and organic conic formulations are a key component in this process. However, generating these formulations can be very challenging, especially when working with nonlinear problems. This paper introduces Hypatia, a new algorithm designed to generate conic formulations from a broad class of challenging nonlinear models, specifically focusing on organic conic formulations. We believe that this algorithm will be particularly useful for addressing complex global optimization tasks, where valid formulations are essential, and provide the algorithm as a part of the Hypatia Julia package for general nonlinear optimization problems, global optimization problems, and convex optimization problems. We also include a discussion on the relationship between Hypatia and existing methods, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm by applying it to a range of difficult optimization problems. The code for the Hypatia package is available online at https://github.com/JuliaOpt/Hypatia.jl. The current version of the algorithm handles only a limited form of nonlinear models, and we outline a number of potential extensions to the algorithm, including integrating it with existing global optimization solvers, and developing methods for efficiently generating conic formulations from linear models. The most recent version of this paper can be found at arXiv preprint at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02742. The advent of deep learning has made it possible to automate MRI data preprocessing, leading to enhanced performance in subsequent processing tasks. However, the lack of a uniform standard for MRI data collection contributes to deep learning models struggling to generalize effectively. This problem is particularly pronounced in the field of neuroimaging, where small changes in data are associated with low generalization dimensions. To overcome this challenge, we propose a strategy that combines data collection dimensions into generalization dimensions through clustering and weighting, making it suitable for a wide range of MRI datasets, including those used for quality assurance in cerebral MRI imaging. We demonstrate this approach's effectiveness by utilizing a small dataset to train a deep learning model for removing chemical shift artifacts in cerebral MRI images and comparing it to a large dataset-based model. The results show that the proposed method's performance is comparable to that of a model trained on a vast dataset for both low and high generalization dimensions. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghraoui/cluster_generalization.

To analyze the impact of private electric vehicles on a power grid's resilience, we developed a novel method that utilizes multi-agent optimization. This approach allows us to evaluate the influence of individual EV owners' behavior on the grid's stability and repair costs following a disturbance. We introduced a new performance measure, dubbed'resilience cost,' that incorporates the financial costs associated with conducting restoration and the discomfort experienced by customers as a result of load shedding or redistribution. Furthermore, we accounted for the uncertain duration of a disturbance and the limited access that distribution companies have to information about individual customers' preferences and charging habits. To validate our method, we conducted case studies in two different scenarios: one with a limited number of private EV chargers and another with a more extensive penetration of EVs in the community. Our results show that private EVs behave differently when owned by high or low income individuals and that they exhibit distinct patterns of charging and displacement of traditional generators depending on whether they are connected to a fast or slow charger. We also discovered that private EVs charged at home during the day can sometimes worsen the grid's resilience, whereas those charged at night or at slow chargers generally improve the grid's resilience. We further found that private EVs can significantly influence the distribution of performance-based incentives offered by the grid operator as they affect the grid's repair costs and, in turn, influence the distribution of these incentives among customers. We also discovered that private EVs charged at home during the day can sometimes worsen the grid's resilience, whereas those charged at night or at slow chargers generally improve the grid's resilience. We also found that private EVs can influence the distribution of performance-based incentives offered by the grid operator as they affect the grid's repair costs and, in turn, influence the distribution of these incentives among customers. We also investigated the effectiveness of different policies aimed at improving the grid's resilience and managing its finances, such as implementing time-of-use electricity pricing, providing free or discounted public charging, offering performance-based incentives to customers, and recruiting'resilient' EV owners who are willing to charge their vehicles during the day. We found that the most effective policy varies depending on the specific context in which it is applied. We also investigated the likelihood of a distribution system operator overstaying or understaying the optimal level of repair effort and its consequences on the grid's resilience and finances. We found that the risk of overstaying or understaying the optimal level of repair effort is higher when the duration of a disturbance is shorter than the time it takes to switch

The number of agents involved in meetings can make decision-making processes increasingly complicated. To simplify this challenge, it's suggested that meetings be divided into distinct phases, consisting of an initial exploration period followed by a more structured decision-making phase. Research has previously focused on centralized, multi-phase decision-making models. In contrast, this study explores a decentralized, multi-phase strategy where individual agents operate independently and make choices within their own defined time frames. A key innovation of this approach is the introduction of a performance phase that allows for the refinement of initial decisions made during the exploration period. A distinctive feature of the model is a complex, multi-agent payoff function that encourages cooperation and drives meaningful interaction among participants. A notable aspect of the payoff function is the presence of external influences that impact the performance phase but cannot be altered by the agents. A novel algorithm has been developed to simulate meetings and a competitive game theory approach has been used to validate the model. A notable finding of this study is that cooperation can be fragile, and even small changes in parameters that affect the payoffs or time frames available to agents can lead to the breakdown of collaboration. A central aspect of the model has been compared to a similar, previously published multi-phase agent model, with the result showing that the current model excels at achieving optimal outcomes but falls short of ensuring the diversity of solutions is maintained. A key achievement of this research is the development of a novel, nonlinear representation of the pay-to-stay/leave threshold, which is a novel approach in the field of complex decision-making. A distinctive feature of the model is the presence of different payoff trajectories for individual agents, with some experiencing continuous decline while others reach a steady state. A novel approach of this study involves comparing the payoffs of agents with the payoffs of an external reference system, with the result showing that the diversity of solutions can be maintained by matching the payoffs of agents with the payoffs of the external reference system, with the result leading to the emergence of optimal outcomes in meetings. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3 and CmSn3, as well as the magnetic characteristics of GdxCm1-xSn3 for x=0.5 and x=1. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on GdSn3 and predict CmSn3 to be a half-metal with a highly conducting 5d Cm layer. Furthermore, we found that the magnetic moment in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series primarily depends on the concentration of Gd and Cm, and that this series exhibits both half-metallic and ferromagnetic characteristics. Our study indicates the potential of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series for novel electronic applications and suggests that by adjusting the concentration of Gd and Cm, as well as using monolayer and bilayer structures, materials with suitable band gaps could be created. If physics beyond the standard model involves a sequence of symmetries similar to those in the standard model, it's conceivable that additional baryon and meson particles could emerge as the fundamental building blocks of matter. This talk will delve into the predictions of extra baryons and mesons that result from extending the standard model's symmetries. We will be reviewing the findings of a previous study that hypothesized the standard model's SU(2) x U(1) gauge symmetry could be expanded to a semi-simple gauge symmetry, possibly in the form of SO(10), E$_{6}$, or SO(18), which could give rise to additional baryons and mesons. Although the predictions of these models often overlap, they did exhibit distinct particles that could be detected at various energy levels, ranging from the current LHC to future colliders like the CLIC and ILC at high energies. We will also be discussing the potential for hidden sector extra baryons and mesons that could result from a sequence of symmetries similar to the standard model, which could affect the vacuum energy density and thus influence the standard model's vacuum stability. Additionally, we will be exploring the predictions of a particular study that involved extending the standard model's symmetries to a sequence of SO(2) x SO(2) x U(1), which could give rise to extra baryons and mesons that may have masses within the reach of current experiments or future colliders. We will be concluding this talk by reviewing the diverse range of extra baryons and mesons that could result from extending the standard model's symmetries, which may emerge as particle pairs that could be detected at the LHC or future colliders, or could be stabilized by a sequence of symmetries that affects the standard model's vacuum stability. This could also pave the way for predicting the masses of extra baryons and mesons that result from a sequence of symmetries similar to the standard model, which may be influenced by the energy scales of new physics beyond the standard model, which could be explored through various approaches including vacuum stability, electroweak symmetry breaking, and the standard model's vacuum stability in the context of cosmology. We will be presenting tables that outline the predictions of extra baryons and mesons that result from extending the standard model's symmetries, which could be compared to the findings of other studies, which may also be accessible at the LHC or future colliders, which may also emerge

The Coxeter group foundation theorem, initially proven by Bouscaren and Reutenauer in 2002 for the A and B types, and by the current author in 2019 for the C type, is shown to generalize to all non-cyclic, finite simple groups based on exchange graph properties. This generalization demonstrates that any element in these groups that is not part of a conjugacy class containing a cycle can be expressed as a product of cycles with specific configuration criteria. Furthermore, this achievement extends the result of the 2009 study by the current author, which established a connection between the foundation theorem and the classification of the finite simple groups based on their exchange graph types. A distinct approach is used to generalize the foundation theorem, different from the original proof, and it leads to a deeper understanding of the group element expression. A statistical analysis of the number series associated with the B-type Coxeter groups reveals an interesting pattern where the associated polynomial factors can be determined for a specific group size for the first time. This advancement is used to generalize the result from the 2009 study to the B-type Coxeter groups. A comprehensive examination is performed on the exchange graph property of a random matrix with a specific distribution, which leads to a probabilistic interpretation of the foundation theorem. The connection between weak lensing gravitational potential and Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) via lensing magnification and luminosity distance modification is investigated. A novel method is presented for calculating the effect of lensing on SNe Ia within the Pantheon dataset. The approach takes into consideration the effects of lensing on both the flux and luminosity of SNe I a. The analysis of the Pantheon dataset reveals an average lensing effect per SN Ia of $0.018_{-0.003}^{+0.004}$ magnitudes and $0.076_{-0.014}^{+0.020}$ magnitudes for a full-wave lensing distortion, which is consistent with the standard model. Furthermore, the study finds that the distribution of the lensing effects is reproducible using a combination of standard cosmological parameters and mass-energy density models of dark matter and matter. The findings are sensitive to the composition of the universe, specifically the $\Omega_m$ and $\Omega_\Lambda$ values. The analysis of the Pantheon dataset for type Ia supernovae considered here is analogous to the analysis of SNe Ia in the standard model, yet the approach differs from the conventional method of SN Ia cosmology due to the effect of lensing. The standard deviation of the lensing effect per SN Ia is found to be $0.226_{-0.043}^{+0.063}$, which is influenced by the mass-energy density of the universe and the distribution of the mass-energy density within the universe. The investigation highlights the potential of SNe Ia data for measuring the matter-energy density distribution within the universe, and the effect could be confirmed with future surveys such as LSST, Euclid, and WFIRST, which will significantly enhance the precision of the calculation to $0.090$ or better. The approach discussed here is applicable to other supernova datasets including the JLA and future datasets from SN Ia surveys. The incorporation of additional factors that influence the lensing effect on SN Ia, such as the effects of strong lensing and megamaser lensing, along with the lensing effects on supernova spectra and photometry, will further contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the universe. The methodology presented in this paper is relevant to other cosmic probes that involve the analysis of modified signals from cosmic objects via lensing effects. The development of efficient and narrow-band light management systems is a growing area of interest for silicon photonics. Despite advancements, expanding these systems to multiple wavelength channels while maintaining compact size poses a significant challenge. This issue can be addressed by creating a 2D T-junction structure on a silicon-on-dielectric material surface, where precise control over light interaction allows for multiple channel crossovers and 1xN splitters within an ultra-compact footprint. This advance paves the way for scalable and compact light management systems across a range of applications. Moreover, this technology can be integrated into existing silicon photonics platforms with minimal modifications, providing a versatile solution for various channels, including long-haul transmission, sensing, and biomedical applications that require low loss and wide dynamic wavelength range. Moreover, this research demonstrates a 10-channel demo, where a 1x10 T hub is combined with a CMOS photodetector to manage high-speed data across a wide spectral range. This achievement also enables the development of complex T hubs, including those with large fan-out, cross, and loop structures, by utilizing a novel etching process that combines dry and wet etching methods, providing a means for adapting this technology to different material platforms. This breakthrough has the potential to influence a broad range of silicon photonic technologies, from high-speed communication to biomedical imaging, by extending light management capabilities across a wide spectral range, enabling low-loss light transmission across different material interfaces, and expanding silicon photonic memory storage capacity. This development opens up a wide range of possible research avenues, including the integration of metal resonators, nanomechanical devices, and hyper-spectral T hubs that cover multiple wavelength channels in both parallel and serial configurations. This technology is compatible with existing silicon photonic foundry processes and provides design rules for various fabrication platforms, including CMOS, SOI, and 3D integration, by offering a versatile T hub builder tool that allows for complex light structure design within a compact footprint. This research paves the way for breakthroughs in a range of biophotonic applications, from imaging and sensing to photothermal cancer treatment, as well as in advanced communication systems, including quantum key distribution, and in the development of complex light structures and material interfaces, including nano/micro resonators, metamaterials, photonic crystal, graphene, and 2D/3D photonic/photonic hybrid structures. The main objectives of this work include proving the existence and categorization of multiple solutions to the mentioned PDE, as well as establishing the continuity of these solutions in relation to the changeable parameter $\gamma$. Additionally, we establish an important result indicating that the singular Kirchhoff PDE is capable of being approximated by a modified Allen-Cahn PDE, with the singular Trudenger-Moser condition, within the domain U. The main tools employed in this proof involve the Mountain Pass Lemma, the Trudenger-Moser inequality, and the Kirchhoff PDE's variational structure. Moreover, we establish the compactness of the solution maps by employing the degree theory, the Kirchhoff PDE's variational structure, and the boundedness of the potential operator. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of the form $f(\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i})$ where $X_{i}$ represents a sequence of independently generated random variables from a subgaussian distribution with a varying mean, denoted as $\mu_{i}$. It is shown that the concentration of $f(\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i})$ around its expected value is characterized by a single-disparity term that takes into account the vector $\mathbf{\mu}$ consisting of the means $\mu_{i}$ and provides a bound on the moment of order $p$ of the functional, i.e., $|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{i}|^{p}$. This leads to a discrete version of a well-known hypercontractive inequality and facilitates achievable rates in certain functional estimation problems. Additionally, a regularized version of this result is presented to handle misspecification of the distribution. Lastly, a specific example involving a Bernoulli distribution with a changing parameter is analyzed to demonstrate the applicability of these results. The study builds upon previous work by C. Bousse-Fleurian and R. Cont, as well as the findings by T. Leli\`evre, T. Seidel, and L. Massouli\`e, by providing a more general and carefully chosen vector $\mathbf{\mu}$ that leads to a sharper bound, and also offers a distinct proof using a combination of subgaussian concentration and the hypercontractive inequality. The proposed approach can be extended to a broader class of functions and extends the application of the result to the analysis of the concentration of the empirical risk minimization algorithm. The paper also discusses connections with the regularized inverse contrast method and the stochastic version of the result, as well as the difficulty that arises when the vector $\mathbf{\mu}$ contains an interior point. The study further examines the difficulty by providing an alternative bound that eliminates the difficulty and leads to the extension of the stochastic version of the result to the regularized inverse contrast method. The proposed approach can be applied to the analysis of the concentration of the empirical risk minimization algorithm and the stochastic version of the result, as well as the regularized inverse contrast method, the stochastic version of the result, and the algorithm, respectively. Given a closed symplectic manifold (M,ω) and a vector field X on M that is tangent to the boundary of M, there exists a local smooth function u, defined in a neighborhood of the zero section in the cotangent bundle T*M, such that its symplectic form ωu is the pullback of ω from M. This result can be rephrased to show that the group of symplectic modifications of a given closed symplectic manifold is in bijective correspondence with the set of vector fields on that manifold that are tangent to its boundary. This implies that the group of symplectic modifications of a given closed orientable surface with genus g is isomorphic to the first homology group of the space of vector fields on a surface with genus g that are tangent to the boundary. Specifically, this yields that the group of symplectic modifications of a given closed orientable surface with genus g is isomorphic to the g-th tensor power of the integral group ring of the cyclic group of order two. This extends the result from a previous paper by Geiges and the author, which addressed the case of surfaces with genus g greater than one. Additionally, it provides an alternative proof of that previous result known as the "Hitchhiker's theorem". Furthermore, it provides an explicit formula to compute the symplectic modification of a given closed symplectic manifold under the assumption that the underlying topological space of that manifold is connected. Finally, it discusses some open problems related to the topological properties of the group of symplectic modifications of a given closed orientable surface with genus g.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word representations learned through neural networks, particularly focusing on the loughran-mcDonald polarity dataset commonly used in NLP research. We initially review the existing methods for assessing the quality of word representations, then explore statistical approaches to determine the level of understanding neural networks have achieved with this dataset. We analyze the distribution of the cosine similarities between word representations and the center points of 12 equally divided polarity dimensions, discovering a normal distribution in the results. We calculate the average distance from the center of each dimension to measure the level of understanding, drawing comparisons with previous research. We also investigate the change in the level of understanding over time as neural networks are re-trained, and find that the results converge to a similar level of understanding. We further split the training and test datasets to estimate the level of understanding for the word representations, calculating this to be approximately 0.87. We believe that this quantitative analysis provides a clear roadmap for evaluating the level of understanding of neural networks in a wide range of NLP tasks. We also apply these statistical measures to a dataset of part-of-speech tags, discovering interesting patterns that reflect the inherent structure of that dataset. We initially proposed these statistical measures in a conference paper titled ``Word Representations Discrete Structure Learning'' presented at the ACL 2020. We hope that this rigorous analysis will be beneficial to the large community of NLP researchers working with neural networks and word representations. We further propose a simple approach to guide the learning of word representations based on their discrete structure, suggesting that this approach leads to improved results in a range of evaluation metrics. We also explore this proposed approach on a dataset of sentiment word representations, discovering that it successfully captures the discrete structure of that dataset. We believe that this proposed approach provides a novel insight into the learning of word representations, offering a unique perspective on the internal workings of neural networks. We further discuss the implications of this analysis for the ongoing debate surrounding the compositionality of neural networks, proposing an intuitive visualization that illustrates the non-compositional nature of the polarity word representations learned through neural networks. We also explore a range of other datasets, discovering evidence of the inherent non-compositional structure present in the datasets of part-of-speech tags, sentiment classifications, and emotional expressions, among others. We believe that this analysis provides a significant contribution to the ongoing discussion surrounding the compositionality of neural networks, offering a unique perspective based on the discrete structure of the datasets with which they are being worked. In multiagent competitions, players' motivations can be driven by a mix of cooperative and self-serving intentions.  When interacting with others, players following a cooperative approach aim to maximize the overall social welfare, whereas those with a self-serving mindset strive to minimize their individual losses.  We examine a strategic problem involving multiple players competing in a combinatorial optimization problem, where agents are rationalizable, meaning their playable actions can be predicted based on a set of feasible solutions and individual loss functions.  We establish a key result showing that, in order to determine a rationalizable equilibrium, it is sufficient to examine a restricted set of high-quality solutions.  However, the size of this restricted set is indicative of the total number of possible solutions multiplied by the number of players.  To overcome this challenge, we develop an approximation algorithm that yields a rationalizable equilibrium comparable to the optimal solution, with a guaranteed performance guarantee linked to the number of players and the optimization problem's dimension.  We further provide a broad-classification result indicating that, under certain conditions, a pure Nash equilibrium can be obtained in games involving combinatorial optimization problems.  In the process of developing these results, we introduce a new approach that involves a projection of an alpha-core that is achievable, and show that this projection is equivalent to the original space.  This is accomplished by demonstrating that the projection's dual space contains the same information as the original space, with the additional feature of being able to define a suitable potential function.  We achieve this by establishing that the set of feasible solutions can be defined by a collection of halfspaces, which allows us to determine the dimension of this space, and thereby obtain a first-order rationalizable equilibrium.  We provide a comprehensive analysis of a general classification of combinatorial optimization problems, along with specific applications to linear programming and submodular maximization.  In the case of linear programming, we show that a pure Nash equilibrium can be obtained when the number of players is less than or equal to the number of dimensions, which is a new result. An analysis of a stochastic SIR epidemic model is performed, using the framework of continuous time random walks on graphs. The model features rewiring of connections in a random network, where links to recently infected individuals are temporarily avoided. The epidemic's spread rate can be determined by the model's parameter settings, resulting in a SIR epidemic dynamics similar to traditional models, with the epidemic's duration being inversely proportional to the spreading rate. Furthermore, the model enables derivation of the final fraction of infected individuals, which varies depending on the spreading rate, and does not exceed 1, unless the average degree of the network is extremely low. The statistics of the epidemic's duration and the number of infected individuals can be determined through the model, which may have applications in understanding real-world networks, including those involving the avoidance of connections between similar cities in transportation networks. The model's results can be compared to simulation data of random immune network epidemics, which were generated using an agent-based model. The model's assumptions can be relaxed, which results in the epidemic's duration being inversely proportional to the square root of the spreading rate, and the statistics of the epidemic's duration and the number of infected individuals becoming deterministic quantities. The model's parameters which break the symmetry of the random network are shown to be proportional to the eigenvalues of the network's configuration matrix, which characterizes the network's community structure. Integrating data from experiments with different underlying assumptions requires adjusting their proton structure function data to a common standard. This process is particularly necessary when combining results from lepton-proton scattering and deep inelastic scattering off nuclear targets. Proton structure functions are calculated from weighted sums of components, consisting of a universal part and components specific to each experiment, which are determined by weight factors. To adjust the data, one must determine the universal components and the weight factors. This theory provides a framework for achieving this data adjustment using physical constraints and consistency requirements, ensuring that the adjusted data preserves its original statistical properties. Although this framework is applicable to general situations, it is primarily designed to facilitate the combination of data from SCER III and OLYMPUS experiments. However, it can be extended to other experimental setups with minor adjustments. This theory framework is suitable for application in numerical form, and it has been implemented in a publicly available code. It is crucial to note that this data adjustment process does not constitute a full fit to proton parton distribution functions. Rather, it is a limited adjustment aimed at correcting for bias introduced when combining results from different scattering processes. As such, it cannot be used as a substitute for traditional proton parton distribution function fits. Nonetheless, it has been found to perform well in predicting scattering off nuclear targets, with predictions differing from actual results by less than 1% relative to the average scattering cross-section. This theory framework has been successfully tested on real data, specifically the combination of results from CLAS and PHENIX experiments scattering off protons and nuclear targets. This has been achieved by integrating the adjusted data into existing proton parton distribution function fits through the use of weighted averages, and comparing the resulting predictions to the actual experimental cross-sections, which showed a less than 1% relative difference. This theory framework provides a suitable method for adjusting proton structure function data at the level of moments, although it has some limitations arising from this approach. These limitations include the loss of critical information related to the underlying dynamics of the scattering process, and the difficulty of preserving certain symmetry properties in the adjusted data. This has implications for analyzing asymmetry components of the scattering cross-section, which are critical for understanding the role of quarks and other substructure components in the scattering process. To improve policy optimization, Variance Reduction Experience Replay (VRER) is proposed, combining variance-reduced online learning and experience replay. This method ensures that the underlying data distribution remains unchanged during training, thereby fixing the weighting scheme used to prioritize samples. Variance reduction is achieved by minimizing the expected loss of the current policy, which effectively modulates the importance of samples. This results in enhanced exploration and a more efficient weighting scheme, capable of adapting to changing data distributions. The advantages of VRER are demonstrated across a range of tasks, showing that it outperforms existing methods when the data distribution changes substantially. Furthermore, VRER is valued for its simplicity, making it suitable for large-scale applications. The code for VRER has been made publicly available. This approach has been successfully applied to both discrete and continuous action spaces. The source code for VRER has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghul131/VRE. The code has also been submitted to the ML Research Repository at https://mlresearchrepository.org/papers/2022/vre-21-12-26.full.pdf. The research underlying VRER has been presented at the NeurIPS 2022 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning and Safety Systems. The experience replay buffer in VRER can be visualized using the tool, VRER Visualization, available at https://vl-research.github.io/vre-visualizer/. The results obtained with VRER have also been compared to those of Rank-1 ER, Rank-5 ER, and BEER, showing that VRER outperforms these methods in almost all the scenarios tested. The challenge of value estimation in VRER is defined as the absolute difference between the expected value of the current policy and the actual value obtained from the experience replay buffer. This challenge decreases as the number of samples increases, making it necessary to balance the number of samples and the efficiency of the algorithm. The results obtained with VRER have also been analyzed in detail, highlighting the factors that influence the performance of this algorithm. The results show that VRER is more efficient when the data distribution changes substantially, but it is less accurate when the number of samples is small. The performance of VRER can be improved by increasing the number of samples, but this incurs a higher computational cost. The results obtained with VRER have been compared to those of the state-of-the-art algorithms in three different scenarios, showing that VRER outperforms these methods in almost all the scenarios tested. In our analysis of chatbots and their limitations, we noticed that their
expected and desired behavior differs significantly. To bridge this gap, we
developed the MultiTalk framework, which enables chatbots to engage in
highly branching dialogues. We believe this framework provides a more
realistic standard for evaluating chatbots, given the typically linear
nature of conversation assessment datasets such as ConvConvAI2. To support
our claims, we created a highly branching dialogue dataset called BranchIt,
along with a simplified version called SimpleBranch. Our findings reveal
that even though chatbots perform poorly on BranchIt compared to ConvConvAI2,
this performance difference diminishes when considering the perspective of
a conversational partner. To demonstrate the utility of MultiTalk, we
implemented a simple chatbot called Branchy using the SubWorld framework,
which produced the BranchIt dataset. To further evaluate Branchy, we created
a customized version of the Expected System Response, a metric that assesses
the expected response of a conversational partner. Branchy's performance
according to this metric shows that it is capable of following a branching
dialogue structure. When comparing Branchy's performance on the SimpleBranch
dataset to ConvConvAI2, we found that the performance difference is minimal. 
In summary, our research indicates that the expected and desired behavior
of chatbots in dialogues that branch significantly is different. To account
for this variation, we developed the MultiTalk framework and created a
dataset called BranchIt. Our findings reveal that the performance of chatbots
on BranchIt is similar to ConvConvAI2 when considering the perspective
of a conversational partner. To demonstrate the utility of MultiTalk, we
implemented a chatbot called Branchy, which produced the BranchIt dataset
and could follow a branching dialogue structure. When comparing Branchy's

A key development in surface growth models is the connection discovered between Gaussian free fields and two-parameter Schramm-Loewner evolution in the subdomain of a planar domain $D$. This discovery extends the initial result by Sheffield, which related a single SLE to a single GFF. The present investigation further builds upon this foundation by proving that multiple SLEs propelled by a log-gas model are equivalent to the local time of a specific Dyson Brownian motion, and this in turn is equivalent to a multi-parameter GFF. The introduction of the two-parameter framework enables a generalization of several specific models, including the relationship between the GFF and a single SLE, as well as the relation between the end-to-end distance of a 1D log-gas and a GFF on the circle. The investigation of these models reveals specific asymptotic behaviors, the most notable of which is the critical correlation length $R_{c}(n)$ for which the expected end-to-end distance of a 1D log-gas on a circle becomes correlated with the GFF on the circle. The investigation demonstrates that $R_{c}(n)$ behaves asymptotically like $\sqrt{2\log n}$. MediaWiki software powers not only Wikipedia but also multiple project websites for various scientific areas such as astronomy, mathematics, and physics. We present WorkingWiki (WW) - a customized version of MediaWiki designed to facilitate collaborative research efforts. WW incorporates features that address typical obstacles scientists face when working together, including the difficulty of integrating raw data, the challenge of synthesizing comprehensive literature reviews, and the need for tailored analytical tools for data and simulations. We highlight WW's potential by demonstrating its application to the research of high-energy particle radiation in atmospheric balloons using MediaWiki's structure to efficiently manage and present results, data sets, and references. The WW source code and an operational demonstration of the particle radiation example are available online. We invite researchers to build upon this framework for their own projects. The WW repository can be accessed at https://github.com/WorkingWiki/WorkingWiki. The particle radiation example website is located at http://particle.western.edu.

We are taking a starting point from the fundamental principle that gravity is a result of non-local curvature, as demonstrated by general relativity's success. General relativity can be described through the Einstein-Hilbert action, which is a local, four-dimensional operation in a manifold $\mathcal{M}$. However, this action cannot be formulated as a variational problem using the metric field directly. Instead, we formulate an action that is in variation with respect to four tetrads, taking into account non-local effects due to tetrads' interactions. This results in a $U(4)$ gauge theory, which reduces to general relativity after implementing a specific $U(4)$ symmetry. This formulation allows for massive spin-2 particles and possesses a consistent non-local gravity sector. Additionally, this formulation enables the determination of a stable ground state through variational methods, which can characterize the universe's state as either empty or containing matter. When the variational parameters differ from those that characterize the vacuum state, a distinctive relativistic propagation speed is observed for massive gravitons. This formulation also provides a predictive approach for predicting the propagation speed of massive gravitons in vacuum, which is a pure theoretical prediction. This prediction can be tested through the analysis of gravitational waves generated during supernova explosions or other highly massive astrophysical events. A distinguishing feature of this formulation is its compatibility with Lorentz invariance, achieved by requiring that the tetrads transform according to a specific connection, which can be thought of as a non-local generalization of the Lorentz group $SO(1,3)$. This is equivalent to postulating that the Lorentz group $SO(1,3)$ is an abstract, gauge symmetry rather than a spacetime symmetry. This formulation has been applied to a simple scalar field theory, resulting in a non-local quantum field theory. This field theory possesses a stable ground state, and the energy spectrum can be determined variationally. The energy spectrum contains contributions from the non-local vacuum energy, particle contributions, as well as the interaction energy between the particle and the non-local vacuum energy. The energy spectrum also includes the energy associated with the propagation of a massive scalar particle, which has a discrete set of possible energies corresponding to different radial vibration modes. Understanding the intricacies of human genetics has become increasingly sophisticated with the integration of new technologies and methods of analysis. This integrated approach has led to a better comprehension of the genome and has produced a wealth of information from sources such as genome-wide association studies and functional genomic data. However, incorporating these advances into a unified framework has been challenging for many researchers. In this paper, an examination of the integrated genome is conducted to be certain that research findings from genome-wide association studies are meaningful and relevant. A novel computational approach was developed to assess the significance of associated genes by incorporating functional genomic data and analyzing the pattern of associated single nucleotide polymorphisms within genes. The developed method was then applied to eighteen human characteristics for which extensive data are available, and the results showed that the majority of characteristic-related genes contain associated single nucleotide polymorphisms that affect expression and are located at specific positions that are crucial for binding, modification, and modification of histone proteins. The integration of genome-wide association study and functional genomic data also enabled the characterization of associated single nucleotide polymorphisms, genes, and non-coding RNA, as well as the identification of key regulatory elements, pathways, and cellular locations that are relevant to these characteristics. The results presented in this paper are available online for further examination and validation by the scientific community. The findings of this research have been published in the journal Nucleic Acids Research and the associated data can be accessed via the website of the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute. The development of the method mentioned in this paper has been made available to the public for download on the Genomic Annotation Analysis website. The integrated genome profiles that were constructed in this research and the associated analysis have been deposited in the NCBI Database of Genomic Variants and the Functional Genomics Database, respectively. The results of this research have also been presented at the ASHG and ESHG conferences, and the data and methods developed in this paper have been licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution license. The method referred to in this paper has been named Genomic Annotation Analysis, and it has been designed to facilitate the examination of genome-wide association study findings, as well as to provide a framework for the prediction of phenotype-relevant genes and the identification of non-coding RNA. The development of Genomic Annotation Analysis was supported by the Canadian Institute of Health Research and the University of Toronto. The development of Genomic Annotation Analysis was also supported by the Canadian Genomics Initiative and the Ontario Genomics Institute. The search for the smallest systems building the universe, such as individual quarks, has an interesting parallel with the largest structures, like galaxies. While these extreme ends are hard to imagine coexisting within the same experiment, there's a theoretical framework that suggests they could be interconnected, reflecting a fundamental symmetry. Quark-gluon states, which are transient and difficult to pinpoint, might serve as these miniature systems' representatives. This talk will delve into the challenges of their direct detection and possible approaches to facilitating their identification in particle collision data. Furthermore, it will also explore the potential for these states to possess properties reflecting the desired symmetry, which could be verified through experiments. Given the LHC's established capability to create such tiny systems through high-energy particle collisions, it's now a matter of developing appropriate analysis tools to extract these states and examine their properties in collision data, such as those from the LHC and future facilities like the Future Circular Collider. This talk will also cover related research, including initial findings from the LHC, and the design of a proposed detector for the Future Circular Collider that's optimized for detecting these subquark systems. This talk is an invitation to explore this uncharted territory in particle physics. Observations of neutron star low-mass X-ray binary systems indicate a variety of repetition patterns for their outbursts, which may be influenced by the binaries' interactions with their surroundings. A new analysis of the repetition intervals of known neutron star low-mass X-ray binary systems reveals that the patterns are generally uniform, although exceptions exist. Specifically, among the galactic population, only the binaries with short repetition intervals (less than 3 years) are uniformly uniform, whereas the remaining systems exhibit both uniformly spaced and randomly varying interval times between outbursts. It is also observed that the repetition patterns are stable for a particular system over time. Furthermore, this study finds that the distribution of repetition intervals is largely independent of the systems' outburst brightness. However, a correlation exists between the distribution of repetition intervals and the systems' outburst character, with systems exhibiting both spaced and sporadic outbursts typically returning to a dormant state for at least a year between outbursts. The research also examines the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary systems located at the Galactic Centre, which are characterized by low outburst brightness and short repetition intervals, repeating in a spaced and sporadic pattern, and suggests these systems may have formed within the Galaxy's star cluster NGC 6624 rather than the Galactic Centre. The study's findings are applicable to black hole low-mass X-ray binary systems and the neutron star and black hole log-nuclear star cluster binaries. Direct and indirect interactions occur between different degrees of freedom in a solid, involving the displacement of atoms, spin, and electrons, and are crucial in understanding various phenomena, from the behavior of light to the stability of magnetic order. The theoretical framework for describing these interactions is established, but calculating their dynamic effects on atoms, molecules, and solids using these interactions, especially on a first-principles basis, poses a significant challenge. In this study, we introduce a method for calculating the dynamic effects of electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational interactions on the positions of atomic and molecular cores, on the distribution of electrons, on the vibrations of atoms, and on the stability of magnetic order, using time-dependent density-functional theory in conjunction with plane-wave density functional theory. By applying this method to various systems, we demonstrate the importance of considering dynamic effects, including the frequency of vibrations, the speed of light, and the finiteness of the system, on the behavior of solids, molecules, and atoms. This approach can be utilized in a range of applications, from the study of chemical reactions and optical properties of molecules and solids to the behavior of electrons and vibrations in nanoscale and bulk materials. By investigating the interactions between electrons, the displacement of atoms, and spin, we gained a deeper understanding of a range of phenomena, from the static and dynamic stability of magnetic order to the dynamics of vibrational modes and electron distribution, including localization and delocalization, and the breakdown of magnetic order due to vibration and the speed of light. This study also highlights the significance of treating core and valence electrons, as well as localized and delocalized electrons, in a unified way, in a range of many-body theories, from time-dependent density-functional theory to dynamical mean-field theory. We further explored the interplay between light, electron, and vibrational interactions, and discovered a new phenomenon of light-induced localization and delocalization of electrons, which could be a universal effect in solids, and demonstrated a potential experiment to observe this phenomenon using existing facilities. Finally, we discussed a range of applications, from the calculation of frequency-dependent electron-vibrational interactions, to the behavior of van Hove singularities, to the dynamics of phonons and plasmons, and concluded by mentioning possible extensions of this approach, including the inclusion of magnetic interactions in time-dependent density-functional theory, and the study of electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational interactions in finite systems using coupled-cluster theory. Different sentence meanings entail distinct connections, as depicted in connections like "puppies are small dogs" and "dogs are often aggressive animals". These diverse meanings are reflected in the varied relations that natural language inference aims to capture. To date, primarily entailing connections have been analyzed within the NLI task. Our study investigates a broader range of connections, including both entailing and contradicting relations, to better understand the underlying properties of language. We analyze two dimensions of variety: the relationships themselves and the sentences' semantic contents. To achieve this, we design a new NLI task that covers both entailing and contradicting relations and explore the variety along the two dimensions using multiple methods, including an automated evaluation and human assessment. Our findings reveal that natural language inference tasks often overlook diverse sentence connections and the complexity of the contents within those connections. We conclude that such a challenging task could serve as a tougher evaluation for various natural language processing systems, including those based on pre-trained models, and propose potential future directions to enhance the evaluation, including a multi-label NLI task and a discourse representation approach. Our data set and systems' codes are available at https://github.com/nyu-dl4oldies/semantic-variety.

This paper explores the potential benefits of using external forces to enhance efficient and resilient bipedal locomotion, citing real-world applications such as wearable robots that generate thrust by stepping on the ground. We examine how the position and orientation of an asymmetric leg, which produces an external force, affects walking stability, energy consumption, and resistance to push disturbances in a simulated environment. The results show that placing the asymmetric leg on the outside of a curved path enhances lateral stability without compromising frontal stability, reduces energy expenditure by as much as 14.6% in comparison to a standard asymmetric biped, and significantly increases the amount of push a biped can withstand before losing balance. We also find that increasing the magnitude of the external force produced by the asymmetric leg leads to a trade-off between energy consumption and resistance to pushes, and that the optimal range for this relationship depends on the composition of the path. Furthermore, in scenarios with curved paths, using the asymmetric leg to produce an external force results in a bi-phasic gait where the biped experiences double the amount of push disturbances before losing balance. We discuss these findings within the context of previous research on bi-stable bipedal robots and gait phase space. Lastly, we examine the resonance that occurs when bipedal movements are not synchronized with the period of the external force, and provide a preliminary analysis of the resonance phenomenon. This investigation highlights the importance of considering the interaction between the biped and its environment when designing resilient and energy-efficient locomotion systems. In the future, we plan to explore methods to stabilize resonant movements, as well as investigate the benefits of using forces generated by stepping to enhance frontally unstable gait. This work is applicable to various real-world scenarios such as wearing robots on both feet that generate thrust by stepping on the ground, and has implications for the design of bi-stable bipedal robots that can move in highly confined spaces. Our primary aim in exploring this relationship is to address the requirements posed by recent advances in additive combinatorial analysis, specifically those of Alon and Munskad, and the theoretical foundations laid down by Bourgain in his work on combinatorial geometry. We demonstrate that a respected field with a complete residue map is necessarily isomorphic to the fractional field of a system of polynomials over a finite field, a result that subsumes and expands upon the results of Alon and Munskad, and Bourgain. We also show that the property of a field being respected is equivalent to it having a "strong residue map", a term that we introduce in this context. Furthermore, we provide a detailed description of the structure of a respected field with a strong residue map, a result that we believe to be innovative in its own right. Alongside these results, we include a straightforward proof of the theorem regarding the independence of systems of polynomials, a result originally proven by Alon and Munskad through the use of combinatorial and probabilistic methods. Lastly, we outline an potential line of inquiry related to the property of a field being "locally respected". All in all, our work is an extension of the work of Bourgain, with results that subsume the results of Alon and Munskad. The detection of gravitational waves at high frequencies is limited by the presence of laser noise in optical interferometric detectors. To overcome this constraint, a novel detector design called sloshing Sagnac interferometer is proposed, aiming to enhance the sensitivity of optical interferometers to gravitational waves in the high-frequency range. This design modifies the geometry of an optical interferometer by adding a moving mass within an optically active resonant cavity. As a result, it generates a stochastic noise-reducing effect due to the non-linear response of the system to laser noise. Furthermore, this design allows for the exploitation of the optical parametric effects in the resonant cavity, such as the generation of a nonlinear phase shift, which can further enhance the signal-to-noise ratio in the high-frequency range. A prototype of this detector, utilizing a few milligrams of moving mass, has been conceptually designed with the possibility of scaling it up to thousands of kilograms. A theoretical analysis indicates that this detector can be optimized to outperform current gravitational wave detectors in the high-frequency range, with the potential to detect specific types of gravitational waves generated by the collapse of rotating star cones. The theoretical analysis has been validated by a numerical simulation of a specific detector, which showed that it can improve the sensitivity to gravitational waves in the frequency range between 10 and 100 Hz. The proposed sloshing Sagnac interferometer can serve as a basis for the development of a more advanced detector, such as the quantum optomechanical sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which has the potential to transition from the detection of gravitational waves to their generation and manipulation. The design of this detector, along with its possible variations, can be applied to other sensing and measurement platforms, such as magnetometry, spectroscopy, and seismic detection, among others. Reconstructing accurate and detailed three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant challenges. This is due to the frequent occurrence of occlusions in images that contain faces, along with the varied lighting conditions and abundant background information present. To address this issue, our research focuses on developing a robust facial reconstruction framework that is capable of aligning and merging multiple views of the same subject with different levels of occlusion. Our self-alignment and self-merge mechanisms ensure that the network automatically identifies and avoids areas that are likely to be occluded. The proposed framework, consisting of two stages, initially generates a broadly aligned three-dimensional face before refining it in the second stage through a group-wise optimization process. The use of a robust adversarial loss function helps enhance the overall quality of the reconstructed model. Our method surpasses the current state-of-the-art methods according to both quantitative and qualitative evaluation criteria. The proposed framework has also been applied to real-world scenarios with limited-view occlusions, resulting in challenging 3D face reconstruction problems. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyangzhang/SADRNet.

A key challenge in the integration of renewable energy sources lies in managing seasonal fluctuations, which can be addressed through the strategic use of storage units. Despite the benefits, many have hesitated to install private energy storage due to uncertainty in pricing and supply/demand. This study assumes that storage is managed autonomously and explores optimal storage sizes for individual households in different contexts, focusing on the distribution system market. A new algorithm is developed to calculate the ideal storage size, taking into consideration various factors including charging/discharging costs, renewable energy generation, and grid constraints. A simplified computer model is used to investigate and compare the atmospheric circulation patterns of various exotic planets described in scientific literature.  The model, which takes into account the effects of atmospheric friction and heat generated by atmospheric interaction with the planet's surface, is applied to hypothetical planets featuring extremely slow, misaligned, and highly turbulent rotation patterns. The model reveals that atmospheric circulation patterns on these planets are controlled by the balance between friction, heat, and the force that keeps the atmosphere attached to the planet, driven by their unique low-pressure regions near the rotation axis. The model also shows that the migration of atmospheric circulation patterns from a slow, one-directional rotation to a turbulent state is highly sensitive to changes in these controlling factors and occurs suddenly in a point of no return. The model is further used to test various parameters on these exotic planets, including the strength of their magnetic fields, surface topography, and the presence of stars' radiation, and the results demonstrate that the model's accuracy can be assured only if the atmosphere is fully simulated, eliminating the need for approximate corrections. The model's applications are demonstrated to potentially exotic planets like those surrounding subgiant stars, brown dwarfs, and giant planets with thick atmospheres. The model's limitations are addressed, and the results are compared to alternative, more complex computer models used to study the circulation patterns of these exotic planets. The model's success in investigating multiple atmospheric circulation patterns on a single computer model has no equivalent in current scientific literature, and its capabilities make it suitable for use in teaching and in demonstrating the interactions between atmospheric circulation patterns and the forces that control them. The model can also be used to investigate multiple planetary circulation patterns on a single computer model, and all the computer code used in this research is available for public use. The research into comparative planetary atmospheric circulation patterns using this model has been continued and the results published in a companion paper.
