To effectively handle real-world conversations, it's crucial to address the issue of over-extensive knowledge retrieval. In this process, we're concentrating on refining knowledge retrieval for open-domain Commonsense Question Answering. We present a novel approach, termed Semantic-Connect via Answer-in-Sight (SCAS), that guides the attention towards more relevant information by incorporating an answer-aware semantic connection objective in addition to a classification task. We also introduce a straightforward strategy called Threshold-SCAS (TSCAS) that incorporates SCAS into a batch learning process, resulting in a more efficient and simplified method. Both SCAS and TSCAS outperform existing models in a range of comprehensive evaluation setups. When applied to real-world conversations, these models demonstrate their ability to engage in more thoughtful responses by selecting information that is more connected to the question and overall more accurate. We further analyze how the connection threshold influences the performance of TSCAS and discover that a higher threshold generally leads to a more rigorous standard and better overall performance. We publicly release our code and models at https://github.com/THUHRL/HRL.

This paper introduces the Random Stroll Method (RSM) to address challenges in Federated Learning (FL) across diverse data. Since data heterogeneity leads to significant difficulties in convergence and performance, FL models typically require robust optimization algorithms to achieve satisfactory results. However, such optimization algorithms typically struggle with extreme data heterogeneity. The Random Stroll Method takes a different approach by simply taking random steps in the direction of updates received from cooperating parties. The algorithmic simplicity of RSM makes it computationally efficient and capable of withstanding extremely diverse data. Knowledge Tracing (KT) addresses the challenge of modeling an individual's knowledge structure based on their interactive history with a computerized adaptive system. This structure can be utilized to create personalized learning paths and optimize the system's adaptivity. As KT research has been successful, its potential uses have expanded to areas beyond computer-adaptive learning, such as system optimization, group-level analysis, and knowledge assessment. Despite these applications, evaluating KT systems remains difficult and time-consuming. To facilitate this process, a Python-based platform called pyKT is presented, which provides a simple and efficient method for evaluating KT systems using deep learning-based methods. pyKT offers multiple KT models, including explicit, implicit, dynamic, and reinforcement learning-based methods, as well as a straightforward way to experiment with various KT systems and evaluate their performance using standard metrics. The benefits of pyKT are demonstrated by implementing the Deep Knowledge Tracing model, which shows that using a simple learning rate of 0.1 for 10 epochs yields a performance similar to the current state-of-the-art. The platform and model findings are validated through a system optimization task and group-level analysis. The results are available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04346. Creating effective proof systems for SMT solvers involves a delicate balance in designing a format that is both convenient for users and soluble for verifiers. A perfect format would be both easy to formulate and easy to validate, but experience shows this balance cannot be achieved and some trade-offs are necessary. In response to this challenge, we present Alethe, a proof format tailored for SMT solvers that facilitates user-friendly proofs and a broadly applicable verification framework. Unlike the current standard, CVC, the Alethe format allows for multiple first-order logic proof structures, including sequents from the installed YAKPT system, and enables user-solver interactions with verifiable logs, all while remaining soluble for a wide range of theorem provers, including linear solvers like DLV and certain branching solvers like Sat4j. Furthermore, the Alethe format includes a simple, executable representation of proofs that can be used for user-solver interactions and proves significantly more efficient for user-formulation compared to CVC, based on an evaluation involving 12 different SMT solvers. Lastly, Alethe proves an accessible and easy-to-use format for user-solver interactions and solvable for a wide range of verification systems, demonstrating an appealing balance between user convenience and solver solubility. In response to the challenge of defining the best proof structure, we propose a method for automatically converting an unresolved proof problem into a corresponding validation problem, thereby enabling the use of a broadly applicable verification framework in conjunction with any SMT solver. We hope the Alethe format and our proof conversion method will serve as valuable resources for SMT solver developers and the research community more broadly. In addition to its utility as an SMT proof format, the Alethe system provides a basic framework for user-solver interactions with verifiable logs, available for reuse by the research community. This paper introduces two innovative developments in Federated Learning with Buffered Synchronous Aggregation.  First, we get rid of the assumption that gradient updates must be constrained within a specific range, making the framework more practical for real-world applications.  Additionally, we impose no limitations on the time it takes for participants to submit their updated gradients, enabling a more flexible scheduling system.  We have also established theoretical guarantees for the optimal learning rate and a unified stopping criterion for participants, allowing them to determine the suitable moment for submitting their updated gradients.  In a range of scenarios, including those with non-linear relationships and time-varying data, we have tested the efficacy of our framework against baseline methods, utilizing synthetic data generated by simulation and actual experimental results from smartphones.  Our findings have been compared to existing techniques, demonstrating the advantages of our approach.  We have made available the code for our proposed method on GitHub at https://github.com/linguogeek/Buffered-FedProx. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across languages with no prior knowledge of the target language. This approach uses a trained neural automatic speech recognition model in a source language as the initial model, fine-tuning it for the target language. There are two primary aspects of transfer learning mentioned in this paper: first, we explore aspeech recognition system's development that progresses from rough to detailed, starting with a source-language model and culminating in a target-language model with large amounts of data and advanced feature extraction techniques; second, we investigate cross-language transfer by developing a German-to-English neural speech recognition system. We successfully trained a neural aspeech recognition system for English using a German training set, outperforming a system trained from scratch on the same data. We also analysed different approaches and found that using a deep learning-based German speech feature extraction technique delivers the best results, achieving an 8.7% reduction in word error rate compared to the baseline. We made our code and data available at github.com/rougher/aiv-nelson.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error rectification models rely on vast amounts of labeled data for multiple domains. However, achieving domain agility with limited resources is a critical goal. This paper introduces a new approach in the context of GER, leveraging meta-learning to transfer knowledge between domains with minimal examples. The proposed method involves training a model in a meta-learning framework with two processes: an initialization phase using vast amounts of data for a primary language domain, and a fine-tuning phase on a small dataset for a target domain. The resulting model is able to effectively rectify errors in a new domain after seeing just 5 labeled examples. The proposed approach achieves strong performance when trained on a single domain and shows significant improvements when transferring to a new domain. This paper also explores multi-domain training, establishing a new baseline in the context of NGLUE. The code and model will be made available to the public.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning runs into issues due to the presence of opposing actions in the data, as it tries to incorporate experiences from all trajectories equally. In response, a new method is proposed that focuses only on successful data trajectories, incorporating a concept we call "positive trajectories." The approach uses a combination of reinforcement learning and a policy regularization technique to handle the diversity of data trajectories. Unlike existing offline learning methods, successful experiences are prioritized over unsuccessful ones, enabling the policy to learn from the best trajectories and ignore counterproductive actions. The proposed technique is further integrated into a simple decision-making model called Positive Trajectory Exploitation (PTE), which maximizes the cumulative reward by selectively selecting successful trajectories. Experiments across a range of offline learning scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, comparing favorably to existing techniques. The approach is feasible to scale, both in terms of data and number of agents, without sacrificing overall performance. The code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/happy-song/Positive-Trajectory-Exploitation.

We developed a novel approach for aligning MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. The method compares aligned and random MV image pairs to train the network, leveraging contrast-enhanced TV images as a golden standard. We tested the network on pairs of images featuring the human head treated with radiation therapy and obtained promising registration results, compared to a gradient-based method. The 2D network yielded a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.89, while the 3D network achieved a DSC of 0.83. The evaluation revealed that our method excels particularly in scenarios where the quality of MV images is suboptimal. The convolutional architecture allows the network to learn image features directly, bypassing the need for explicit feature extraction. We utilized a lightweight design to ensure the network's scalability for larger, more complex datasets. The code and model are available for public use. As a result, there is a growing interest in Federated Learning (FL) and Blockchain (BC) technology within this field. V392 Persei, observed in 2016, is a gamma-ray emitting nova.  Novae like this are gas expelling events from a binary system, where a white dwarf is surrounded by an accreting companion.  V392 Persei, which reached magnitude 5.7, is notable for being the second nova detected in gamma-rays and the first from a dwarf nova.  Although a two-year wait is common for observing the nova ejecta, V392 Persei's ejecta were seen one year after the explosion, a rare occurrence. Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a cutting-edge text-based game simulator built using Python and the TextWorld framework, which enables the rapid exploration of generated levels by assigning actions to be dictated by mathematical formulas rather than descriptive language. Our findings show that leveling speed increases dramatically when using a linear approach, with a million moves now possible in just one second, and level generation becomes extremely fast with a hundred levels possible in a single second. Although challenging, we succeeded in creating a linear text-based game by hand, which can be played at an astonishing speed of twenty thousand moves per second. Our research offers TextWorldExpress as a useful tool for developing high-speed benchmarks in fields like text generation and provides pre-existing linear text-based game examples for public use. Our research has been made available on GitHub at the following location: https://github.com/PranavT/TextWorldExpress.

The interplay of light, electrons, and nuclei within solids allows for the intricate interrelation of electromagnetic resonance, electronic states, and nuclear properties.  This overlap enables the sophisticated study of matter, utilizing techniques like resonant x-ray scattering (RXS).  Despite the mechanical nature of nuclear motions, which complicates the precise alignment of nuclear phases with x-ray illumination, a new idea has emerged for directly measuring nuclear phases using RXS.  This approach leverages the precise alignment of the electric field vector with the spin of the scattered electrons to extract detailed information about nuclear phases, levels, and symmetries.  By exploiting the established relationships between magnetic resonance and the initial conditions of nuclear motions, researchers can reconstruct the underlying phase structure of materials, even in presence of thermal fluctuations or nuclear magnetic resonance.  This novel perspective on x-ray scattering emphasizes the critical connection between magnetic resonance, nuclear phases, and the electronic and crystallographic properties of materials, facilitating the implementation of phase-recovery algorithms to extract accurate nuclear phases, levels, and levels densities from RXS data.  The successful application of this method has been demonstrated in an investigation of the interplay between electronics and nuclear motions in an antiferromagnetic compound, known as strontium orthoferrite, for the first time revealing the detailed level structure of the nuclear phase space in a solid.  This breakthrough opens up the promising use of x-ray scattering as a quantitative, real-time sensor of nuclear phases, levels, and scattering levels densities, allowing for the direct recovery of nuclear phases from scattering intensities, and providing a rich, chemical and physical parameter for data analysis, analogous to electronic or magnetic phases.  The developed RXS phase-recovery framework is versatile, and has been implemented using the exact algebraic formulation of the RXS scattering intensities, exploiting the overcomplete set of RXS basis operators, allowing it to be applicable to a broad range of materials and scattering geometries.  The framework has been successfully tested for its robustness against noisy data, as well as its ability to recover accurate nuclear phases, levels, and levels densities from simulated RXS data of an ideal crystal, incorporating thermal fluctuations or nuclear magnetic resonance, and has also been implemented using the numerical integration of the RXS scattering intensities, providing results that are in excellent agreement with the exact algebraic formulation. In written communication between humans and AI, certain discourse markers such as "however" and "nevertheless" convey similar meanings, prompting the question of whether necessary. Currently, available datasets fail to account for the diverse functions and variations of discourse indicators, which hinders the performance of automatic sentence ranking systems. To address this limitation, we present a novel method for assigning a relevant modification to incoming text based on its discourse indicators, with the goal of evaluating the functionality of these indicators in subsequent sentences. We have created a new dataset, DiscSense, which comprises sentences with discourse indicators that have been labeled for desired modifications by a machine learning model. Human assessors then evaluated the predicted modifications for plausibility and validated the existing datasets' representation of discourse indicators' functions. Both sets of results reveal a a a gap in the existing datasets, with certain indicators's functions (such as "by contrast") being overrepresented while others (such as "given that") are rare or missing. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we used the DiscSense dataset to conduct a range of experiments, including validation of the existing datasets, a search space reduction task, and automatic sentence ranking. The results show that DiscSense is a comprehensive and diverse dataset that exceeds the existing datasets in terms of density, with 27 different discourse indicators' functions being captured, compared to the 14 listed in standard reference materials. Furthermore, our approach outperforms the existing method for search space reduction and ranking system evaluation system, known as BART, which relies solely on statistical properties. The code and dataset for DiscSense are available at the following link: https://github.com/DeepTextLabs/DiscSense.

We investigate matrix decomposition problems under a fixed-rank constraint, which can be viewed as an optimization problem on a Grassmannian manifold. We show that a wide class of matrix decomposition problems with a fixed-rank constraint yield geodesically convex objective functions. Furthermore, we determine the conditions under which the Hessian matrix of these objectives vanishes on a distributionally closed subset of the Grassmannian manifold. We analyze various optimization problems, including trace ratio maximization, trace ratio minimization, quadratic optimization, and logistic regression, on the Grassmannian manifold. We demonstrate that these problems can be reformulated as second-order cone programs, making them easily solvable using established methods. We also explore and justify the geodesic convexity of these optimization problems from a Riemannian viewpoint. For general matrix decomposition problems, we establish the connection between the Riemannian Hessian and the Euclidean Hessian, which is crucial in defining the geodesic convexity of these problems. We then provide a critical examination of the matrix decomposition problems, identifying their convexity properties and discussing the Riemannian Hessian analysis. We conclude by investigating the relation between the distributionally closed set and the solution spaces of these optimization problems and present several numerical examples to demonstrate the effectiveness of these models. We also append a list of open research questions in this domain. Lastly, we make our code available online. We believe this work contributes significantly to the field of fixed-rank optimization, offering novel perspectives, new results, and promising research directions. We anticipate this work will inspire further research and provide valuable insights for the community. We intend for this document to serve as an introductory resource for researchers new to fixed-rank optimization and as a reference for experienced researchers in the field. Our study examined the convergence to a Nash equilibrium by analyzing the perception population's impact on generation gaps, the effect of different perception population sizes, the presence of random initial production levels, and the influence of players' memory in repeated games. Our research showed that a diverse perception population accelerates the evolution towards a Nash equilibrium, that the population's diversity changes over time, that a certain level of random initial production levels is necessary for faster convergence, and that the presence of random interactions among players disrupts the convergence process. Furthermore, we found that players' memory plays a crucial role in repeated games, and that there are different dynamics governing the variation of the population in one-shot and repeated games. Our study also highlighted the importance of proper normalization in the genetic variation of the perception population, and the presence of multiple Nash equilibria in some scenarios. Our research used a simple model with a continuous fitness function and explored two variants involving a gap-based fitness function with a threshold, and a hybrid approach combining elements of both. Convolutional Neural Networks are prone to security breaches when exposed to maliciously crafted input that causes hardware failures, leading to side-channel leaks and inaccurate classifications. To ensure the stability of these networks, we recommend checking the validity of input data against failed hardware constraints before feeding it into the network. In this study, we focus on a specific hardware failure caused by an image processing constraint known as Debriefing-Resizing, which involves checking the size of image regions after feature extraction. We develop a range monitoring system that tracks the dimensions of image areas and validates them against predetermined limits. The tested model demonstrates high accuracy while experiencing hardware failures, and our range monitoring system enhances its stability in such conditions. Furthermore, our research highlights an important application of activation validation in low-resolution image processing. We have made our code available online for public use. Additionally, we propose a novel approach called Resolution-Resizing, which refines the Debriefing-Resizing method by scaling the network's resolution dynamically. This study and our code have been published at the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) in 2021 under the topic of Deep Learning Robustness Against Hardware Failure. The proposed validation method has also been successfully applied to other static constraints in image pre-processing. Our approach creates a unified framework for translating between multiple languages by organizing words into shared semantic clusters, which are consistent across different languages.  This cluster-based structure facilitates translations by allowing words in one language to be matched to multiple equivalent words in another language that reside in the same cluster.  We developed the BICRW method, which uses a bias-removed word representation to create clusters that enable cross-lingual equivalence, even for words that have no direct translation.  The clusters produced by BICRW showcase the implicit relationships between words in each language, showcasing multiple degrees of equivalence.  We showcased the effectiveness of this approach in both translation and word selection tasks, demonstrating a significant enhancement over existing methods.  The code for BICRW is available at https://github.com/Chengmin-OU/ACL-21-BICRW.

This paper presents measurements of pions, kaons, protons, and photons produced in Xe-Xe collisions at a 5.44 TeV collision energy, courtesy of the ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC. These findings extend our knowledge of central heavy-ion collisions, particularly regarding transverse momentum patterns, yield gradients, and particle ratios. A comparison with Ru-Ru collisions at the same collision energy reveals similarities in particle ratio gradients but distinct patterns in yield gradients. Furthermore, these measurements enable the creation of pion-kaon ratios across a range of transverse momenta in proton-proton collisions at the same energy, demonstrating consistency with power-law trends observed in higher-energy collisions. A detailed analysis of pion-proton ratios in various collision systems across a broad transverse momentum range reveals the underlying physics required to explain the observed patterns, likely involving combinations of hadron gas thermodynamics and quark-gluon plasma medium effects. A special case is examined, involving the measurement of $\phi$ meson yields in Xe-Xe and Ru-Ru collisions, which may be influenced by $\Omega$ meson production and underlying hadron fragmentation processes. A comprehensive theoretical framework from the TRENTO model is employed to interpret these results, offering valuable insights into initial conditions, medium response functions, and hadron formation mechanisms. A unique aspect of this study involves the integration of experimental and theoretical results, yielding a deeper understanding of collision systems and contributing to the development of a general framework for describing heavy-ion collisions. A special appendix is included, detailing the analysis of proton and neutron fragmentation functions in colliding hadron matter. Recently, visual-inertial navigation methods have demonstrated high precision in navigating indoor environments with multiple cameras and IMUs. These systems typically employ neural network filters that combine visual and inertial measurements, and typically don't utilize the inherent properties of inertial signals in their models. In response to these observations, a new external memory attention-based method is presented for visual-inertial navigation. This approach leverages the unique characteristics of inertial signals to inform the attention model, enabling the external memory to focus on the most relevant time periods and sensory inputs. By tuning the proposed method's parameters, users can either utilize the inherent properties of inertial signals or bypass this feature, demonstrating robustness in doing so. Experiments conducted on a moving robot equipped with an omni-directional camera and two IMUs located at different orientations, navigating through complex environments at varying speeds, showed that the system achieves a localization precision of 0.77 meters using only visual and inertial data, and 0.54 meters when additional GPS and GPS+map data are incorporated. These results are compared to the current state-of-the-art VIO and VIO+GPS baselines, demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed method. The code for this research has been made available at https://github.com/ShuaiNiu1993/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, and in the context of linear dispersion relations, Weyl semimetals can be defined using matrix theory. A bulk Weyl semetal can be characterized by a unique quantum number, and its surface charge density can be determined through the Frobenius theorem in linear algebra. However, extending this concept to nonlinear dispersion relations proves to be challenging. In a new framework, a nonlinear Hamiltonian with an elevated order is proposed, and by utilizing a linear transformation, it can be transformed into a form that defines a nonlinear Weyl semetal. This transformation reveals the exact conditions for realizing a nonlinear Weyl semetal and demonstrates that a specific surface termination can result in a $\Sigma$-shaped contour of the Fermi arc, along with an accumulation of charge density at specific points. Furthermore, this framework enables an analytical calculation of the nonlinear dispersion relation's topological characteristics, which occurs over a relatively broad range of parameters. Moreover, this framework applies to both 2D and 3D systems and predicts that a specific surface termination of a 3D nonlinear Weyl semetal will exhibit a double $\Sigma$-shaped contour of the Fermi arc and an accumulation of charge density at specific points, which occurs generally and is independent of the specific form of the nonlinear Hamiltonian. This framework also provides a precise condition for realizing a point of topological transition between a Dirac semmetal and a nonlinear Weyl semetal. This is a unique and distinct result from the existing theories, which can be tested through experimental measurements of the Landau level spectrum in a honeycomb lattice with next-nearest neighbor interactions. In the context of a federated learning setup, where multiple entities collaborate to create a shared model, our proposed method, Federated Discriminative Aggregation, enhances the efficiency of model development by exploiting the unique characteristics of each data set. Specifically, our approach leverages a discriminative objective function to assign distinct roles to data sets as either sources of new data or assistance in model training, thereby improving performance in comparison to conventional methods. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness across multiple, carefully designed scenarios. Firstly, we compare it to conventional techniques using three well-known classification datasets, with our method showcasing comparable performance when compared to these methods. Secondly, we conduct experiments using a combination of normally distributed data and a real-world customer relationship management dataset, revealing that our method successfully identifies noisy data sets and rejects them as sources of new data. Lastly, we explore the potential of our method in comparing multiple data sets for knowledge integration, finding that it correctly indentifies the most useful data sets. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to assess the impact of material defects, particularly niobium, on quantum coherence due to terahertz radiation. To this end, we employed near-field terahertz spectroscopy to investigate the radiation patterns within coplanant resonators made of superconducting niobium, both with a thick film and a thin film version, and compared the results to simulation findings. The studies revealed that the radiation patterns are essentially unaffected by the transition from a thick to a thin film, with patterns primarily influenced by geometric features. Consequently, the effect of radiative loss on coherence should be similar in both cases. Furthermore, we observed areas of strong radiation close to sharp edges, and these regions around corners may contribute significantly to radiative loss, competing with the effect of defects. To validate this, we measured the average intensity and spectral shape across a range of resonators, finding that the effects of radiation patterns are averaged out and that the energy relaxation time remains unaffected by the radiation patterns. These outcomes have implications for designing resonators with low radiative loss and enhancing coherence by minimizing the impact of sharp edges, not just the surface area. Nonetheless, to confirm these findings on larger scales, similar investigations are necessary on larger resonators made of thin films. Nonetheless, the emergence of near-field terahertz spectroscopy as a powerful analytical tool for quantum devices is clear, offering a direct understanding of terahertz radiation patterns and subsequent coherence loss. This knowledge can be applied to other materials and devices containing complex geometries, and it may be used to optimize the coherence of quantum devices, recovering lost coherence due to radiative loss. Moreover, this approach can be extended to the study of energy and phase error mechanisms in a wide range of quantum systems. Lastly, we discuss the possibility of incorporating sharp edges intentionally to reduce the influence of line defects on coherence. This approach may also be applicable to quantum systems built using combined materials, such as niobium-aluminate, and other integrated quantum systems. The nonlinear Hawkes model, characterized by a system of complex integral equations, is a process by which point processes generate additional points in response to the occurrence of previous points. This model has significant applications in fields such as biology, finance, and sociology. To avoid the computational challenges of its direct use, researchers often rely on linear approximations, but these may diverge significantly from the true nonlinear dynamics. In this paper, a Bayesian method is proposed to assess the nonlinear parameters of a Point Process by utilizing approximate solutions derived from the thin interface limit of the corresponding mean field system. This approach enables estimation of the shape of the activation function, the time-dependent interaction kernel, and the underlying point process itself. Furthermore, the method allows for validation of the nonlinear Hawkes model and the evaluation of its ability to capture complex dynamics. The proposed framework is tested using both synthetic data and a dataset of EEG recordings from humans. The results show that the proposed method effectively estimates the unknown parameters and evaluates the validity of the model, but also highlights issues with the data used. The method, its implementation, and the results have been made publicly available. The proposed Bayesian assessment of the nonlinear Hawkes model provides a valuable tool for future research, and could be adapted for use with other types of time-series data. Quantum error prevention is crucial for maintaining accuracy in computational processes. Rank error checking, a straightforward and efficient protocol, can successfully detect and correct certain types of quantum error. Specifically, it identifies and corrects rank errors on symmetric matrices, which are crucial for implementing unitary operations. Prior research indicated that, with a measurement threshold of $\tau=1$, rank error checking could successfully correct symmetric errors with ranks $r_{in}\leq r_{th}= \lfloor\tau d\rfloor$. However, this standard interpretation overlooks the impact of incremental error growth. As a result, we examine the effect of incremental error growth and find that it leads to a more comprehensive understanding of error growth, which in turn demonstrates that the threshold $r_{th}$ is directly equal to $\tau d$, even in the presence of continuous error generation. Moreover, this interpretation enables us to determine the probability of successful decoding following a measurement outcome, which in turn allows us to introduce a new, more efficient decoding protocol that is effective in correcting errors up to a specific rank threshold. This new protocol is particularly advantageous in implementing unitary operations via amplitude amplification techniques. Our analysis and resulting decoding protocol are both the most advanced and the most comprehensive in the field of error prevention via rank error checking. Nevertheless, there are specific error scenarios that cannot be rectified via this protocol, which in turn highlight the importance of evaluating decay rates, error generation rates, and other relevant parameters in actual implementations. In the context of amplitude amplification, our analysis also examines the probability of successful decoding, which in turn enables us to calculate the overall success probability of unitary operation execution. Our research further demonstrates that the threshold measurement value $\tau d$ must be an integer for successful decoding to occur, which in turn can be achieved by manipulating the dimension $d$ of the error space rather than $\tau$. Our analysis facilitates efficient execution of unitary operations via amplitude amplification by revealing the optimal approach among the following methods for setting the measurement threshold $\tau$: (1) the standard approach, (2) the incremental error growth method, and (3) the dimensions of the error space $d$. Our research provides unique insights into the relationship between error generation rates, decay rates, and the probability of successful decoding, all of which are critical in actual implementations. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye lenses, we propose a concept where multiple lobster-eye lenses are combined to cover a single field of view. Each lens is attached to a separate image sensor, and these sensors are then combined to create a single, more comprehensive image of the field of view. By minimizing the number of image sensors, their total cost can be significantly reduced, in addition to lowering power consumption and increasing durability. Furthermore, a smaller number of image sensors results in a shorter time it takes to read out the image, allowing for faster monitoring of transient X-ray events. We demonstrate this concept using a simulation where a single lobster-eye lens with a 4 square degree field of view is combined with 16 small image sensors, each with a 1 square degree field of view, completely covering a 16 square degree field of view. We show that the point spread function (PSF) of the array is similar to the PSF of a single lobster-eye lens, and that the contrast ratio of the array to a single lobster-eye lens is nearly indistinguishable. We also examine various configurations of the multi-lens array and discuss possible applications in transient X-ray science. Although this concept is particularly suitable for monitors employing lobster-eye lenses, it can be adapted to other types of X-ray optics. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained to classify masked dark matter densities in N-body simulations, and it revealed that the underlying pattern enables reliable prediction of masked densities by simply considering the cosmic speed in the vicinity. When applied to real galaxies, this insight allows for the estimation of hidden dark matter densities and hence the determination of halo masses. Leveraging deep learning is now common for automating data processing tasks, particularly in areas like finance, logistics, and science. However, the practical application of these models is limited by the substantial time and money required to accurately label their training data. This challenge is especially pronounced when working with visually complex documents, like invoices, receipts, and IDs, that need interpretation across different formats and styles. Although research has focused on developing models to extract data from simple documents like forms, there's a significant gap in this regard with respect to more visually rich documents, given the lack of suitable training data available. To address this issue, we introduce a method that employs a bare-bones supervised learning framework to combine model fine-tuning with automated labelling of training data, based on surreptitiously collected anonymous information. This approach allows large models to be fine-tuned for documents without explicit labelling, by utilizing a vast amount of data that's previously been formatted into simple templates. Our experiments on a large-scale dataset consisting of 60 different document classes, show that our approach can reduce labeling expenses by a factor of 50 while achieving a 95th percentile accuracy of 12% and a 95th percentile F1-score of 20% in extracting important data fields. Our method's effectiveness is further demonstrated by a real-world implementation at a large company, where it's used to extract data from millions of documents. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml-ethics/visdoc-extraction. Our approach's capabilities are so versatile that it can be applied to any visually rich document type, as long as there's enough anonymous training data available. Our findings also highlight the practical value of models that can be trained on pseudo-labels, a aspect that requires further research in the deep learning community. Our method can be expensive to set up, as it needs a specialized infrastructure to collect and annotate anonymous training data, but it's highly suitable for custom applications, given its extreme adaptability. Our approach's ability to handle diverse document formats and styles, as well as its ability to handle changes over time, makes it an ideal solution for problems that aren't one-time tasks. Our method can be improved by reducing the amount of data needed for anonymous labelling, as well as by decreasing the time it takes to train the model, which will make it even more practical for real-world applications. To evaluate the impact of physical distancing on urban interactions, this study uses anonymized mobile phone location data from a significant economic hub, Singapore. It analyzes two years of data surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic, a control period before the pandemic, and identifies key patterns of changes in daily interactions within the city. Results show that physical distancing accelerated a shift towards less frequent, longer-duration visits, as users opted for more individual activities. Nevertheless, it also enabled greater exploration of the city, a wider range of visited locations, and more frequent visits to lower-population-density neighborhoods. By examining data on user income levels, the study finds that interactions among lower-income individuals declined more significantly, in terms of both frequency and diversity, than they did for higher-income individuals. Consequently, the existing disparity in urban interactions between higher-income and lower-income individuals widened during the pandemic. Existing research primarily focuses on reduced mobility overall, without delving into disparities in urban interactions. By contrasting different income levels, this study uncovers a previously unexplored aspect of income-based differentiation and offers guidelines for targeted strategies to revive the diverse dimensions of urban interactions affected by the pandemic. Furthermore, its methodology provides a framework for studying the economic and social effects of the pandemic, and other similar events, in various geographical settings. Last but not least, this study's findings are relevant to a wide range of place-managers, policymakers, and researchers alike, who seek to understand and analyze the consequences of physical distancing on a city's economic and social dynamics. A single, unified theory explaining the formation of massive stars is lacking, with different pathways proposed based on whether they form in protostellar disks or through the collapse of dense cores. While the external inflation of massive protostars makes it difficult to determine their mass, their internal structure is well understood and likely involves a rotating, massive disk and a low-density envelope. However, determining whether these protostars accumulated their mass quickly or slowly is challenging. By systematically analyzing the molecular line ratios of massive protostars, we found that the most inflated objects exhibit low ratios, suggesting they have hot, dense gases close to them, possibly indicating a hot disk. This is consistent with models featuring a dense disk and it implies these protostars had a higher accretion rate. Furthermore, we found that the most inflated objects have higher line ratios at higher velocities, indicating they had higher accretion rates in the past. This is supported by observations showing that the most inflated objects are often associated with cometary objects that are likely undergoing mergers. These mergers would result in the injection of energy and mass, leading to a increase in accretion rate and external inflation. This suggests that massive protostars can accumulate their mass through the mergers of dense cores during their formation, rather than through the collapse of a protostellar disk. This could also explain the long formation times of massive stars, as it adds significant time to their development due to the time it takes for these mergers to occur and for their mass to be accumulated. This includes the time it takes for the gas to dissipate following these mergers, which could be similar to the time it takes for low-mass stars to form from their molecular clouds. This theory is supported by the fact that massive stars typically form in clusters, which provides the necessary environment for these mergers to occur. This is consistent with the long formation times of massive stars compared to low-mass stars, as it results in masses that are more consistent with observed values. This could also result in a greater variety of massive star formation pathways, which could be reflected in the different subtypes of massive stars, such as the distinction between types O and L. This includes the possibility of a relationship between their molecular line ratios and the presence of cometary objects, which could be tested using existing and future surveys. For underwater missions within stratified environments, where surface waters mingle with still deeper layers of calm water, ensuring successful navigation is crucial. We've encountered instances where navigation fails due to sudden movements from surface disturbances. To overcome this challenge, we've developed a novel controller that combines sonar sensors operating at different frequencies to detect and adapt to such changes. By utilizing medium-frequency sensors to locate objects and high-frequency sensors to scan the water depth for surface disturbances, we've created a system that prioritizes sensor placement based on distance from the surface and object locations. This strategic placement enhances the controller's performance and reduces failure rates in highly dynamic environments. We've tested and validated our controller on a realistic simulation and a physical robot in a controlled environment, using up to seven sonar sensors simultaneously. These trials have shown significant improvements in successful navigation rates of up to 60% in highly turbulent conditions. We believe this breakthrough has significant potential for expanding the capabilities of underwater robots in a variety of applications. To facilitate further development, we've made the simulator and controller available as open-source tools. We're excited about the possibilities this research enables and invites fellow experts to join forces and contribute to its advancement. The sonar sensor controller currently supports the Sonar Sensor Simulator, a simulation platform that simulates real-time sonar sensors in complex underwater environments. The controller and simulator share the same code, ensuring seamless integration and mutual benefits. The controller and simulator are designed to accommodate a range of sonar sensors, including those with different frequencies, and feature advanced water depth simulation capabilities, complete with surface disturbances, sediment layers, and underwater obstacles. The code for the controller and simulator is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/stratified-ucy/sonar-simulator. The current version of the controller and simulator focuses on navigation with moving objects and surface disturbances, but we're confident it has the potential to adapt to other applications, such as searching for specific objects or optimizing sensor placement. The code for the controller and simulator includes examples of moving and stationary objects, as well as sample scenarios for searching and sensor placement, which can serve as starting points for further development. The development of the controller and simulator has been supported by the University of Cyprus and the European University Institute of Florence. For individuals with visual impairments to navigate safely and independently within unfamiliar indoor spaces, creating and using accurate and detailed navigation maps is crucial. Presently, mainstream methods rely on visual maps and global positioning systems (GPS) for navigation, which are ineffective for those with visual impairments. In response to this challenge, a new concept called HiTMap has been developed, combining topological mapping techniques with hierarchical spatial representation to create a diagrammatic navigation tool. This innovative approach uses a simplified and intuitive graph format to present navigation information, eliminating the need for detailed spatial descriptions. By focusing on a map's topological features, HiTMaps minimize the amount of spatial data required for navigation, resulting in a more compact and user-friendly representation. To evaluate the effectiveness of HiTMaps, a simulation-based assessment was conducted, revealing that they outperform traditional mapping methods in terms of navigation efficiency and overall size. Moreover, HiTMaps have been successfully implemented in a navigation application for a real-world indoor space, demonstrating their practical usability. The HiTMap framework also offers modularity and flexibility, allowing its components to be used separately for other navigation-related purposes. In summary, the HiTMap framework presents a cutting-edge navigation solution specifically designed for individuals with visual impairments, offering a clean and simple representation of navigation diagrams that can be used in a variety of contexts. Full details concerning the HiTMap framework, including its individual components and navigation algorithms, are available in the supplementary documentation attached to this paper. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring minute variations in local magnetic fields, especially in areas with significant electromagnetic noise. Quantum atomic interferometry offers a promising solution for achieving high sensitivity in magnetic field detection. In this research, we propose utilizing superconducting materials to create a stable and controlled environment for measuring the change in magnetic field induced by the Meissner effect. Furthermore, this method can be applied to measure the flux flow resistance, and we show that this approach is suitable for incorporating multiple measurements, enabling us to validate the reliability of our experiment. These achievements pave the way for utilizing this method to monitor local magnetic fields in a controlled environment, and we discuss a specific scenario where this capability can be utilized. High-performance computing on GPUs for object-based programming necessitates an advanced memory allocation system that is both efficient and concurrent. Presently, CUDA provides a limited amount of memory for stack-based allocation, leaving developers to rely heavily on dynamic memory allocation through the `malloc` function, which they can use themselves or acquire from a limited pool of pre-allocated blocks. These approaches, however, introduce performance obstacles due to their sequential nature and inadequate memory usage. In response to these challenges, we present DynaSOAr, a state-of-the-art, concurrent memory allocator for GPU object-based programming. Designed to automate memory management and streamline concurrent allocation and deallocation processes, DynaSOAr includes a novel approach to detecting memory fragmentation, a range of block size options, and specialized locks to enhance performance and efficiency. Furthermore, DynaSOAr features an innovative, predictable stack storage system to optimize memory usage and reduce memory waste. In our tests, DynaSOAr demonstrated substantial gains in performance and memory utilization across a range of applications, including complex object-based GPU programs. We also open-source DynaSOAr to the public, inviting contributors to enhance its capabilities and provide support for new features. Our findings have significant implications for the design of future GPU memory allocators, suggesting that a careful balance between concurrent and sequential operations is crucial for optimizing performance and memory usage in object-based GPU programs. In addition, we present a simple yet effective stack storage system that can be employed across various contexts, including embedded systems, firmware, and software development. Lastly, our experience with DynaSOAr highlights the difficulties of detecting memory fragmentation and integrating locks in memory allocators, posing challenges for their efficient design. In our evaluation of DynaSOAr, we analyzed various metrics, including memory utilization, memory fragmentation, object allocation time, stack storage depth, and lock acquisition time, to demonstrate the allocator's performance and memory usage in real-world applications. We believe that our findings, coupled with the open-source nature of DynaSOAr, will facilitate further development and refinement of this memory allocator, as well as similar concurrent memory allocators for GPU object-based programming. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model, applicable to all impurity states, incorporates the effects of hybridization, magnetic moment, and orbital motion. It yields expressions for the energies and widths of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states, particularly the central and asymmetric states that form in the gap of a superconductor due to the interaction between a magnetic impurity and the surrounding electrons. This framework has been utilized to investigate the YSR states generated by Manganese impurities on the Nb(110) surface, comparing the results to experimental data obtained using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. The simulation reproduces the known behavior of YSR states and predicts additional features associated with combined states, revealing their dependence on the orientation of the magnetic moment and the absence of combined states within the energy gap of the superconductor. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the YSR states formed by a single impurity and a dimer located close to each other exhibit distinct combined states that evolve as the distance between the impurities changes, altering the symmetry of the states and causing them to move across the energy gap of the superconductor. This theoretical analysis agrees with experimental findings and provides a comprehensive understanding of the YSR states and their combined effects in a superconductor, giving insight into the interplay between electron pairing, magnetic moments, and the local symmetry of the impurity states. This understanding can be applied to a wide range of magnetic impurities on a superconducting surface. The code used for this simulation can be accessed at https://git.io/AMScode. In 1993, Erdos, Spinka, and Galvin established a fundamental result in Ramsey theory for infinite graphs, demonstrating that in any coloring of an infinite graph from a two-color palette, at least one monochromatic infinite component exists. Subsequent to this discovery, researchers began exploring variants of this phenomenon, leading to the study of a specific density measure, known as Ramsey upper/dense or top density, and various associated problems in infinite graph theory. Specifically, researchers investigated determining the Ramsey upper density of specific infinite graph structures, as well as properties of infinite graphs that contain arbitrarily large monochromatically colored components with a specified Ramsey upper density. This paper builds upon these prior results by establishing an infinite graph theorem in a two-color Ramsey setting based on upper density, where the ramsey top density of an infinite graph is defined as the highest density at which it contains an arbitrarily large monochromatic component in a two-color Ramsey game. Furthermore, this infinite graph theorem is formulated in three distinct variations, each addressing a different aspect of ramsey top density in infinite graphs. Additionally, this paper provides an alternative proof of an existing result by the research group of Kuhn, Razanska, and Schlegel, as well as a variety of infinite graph structures that have a specific ramsey top density of 1/2. Lastly, this paper concludes by presenting an open problem related to the ramsey top density of infinite trees in a two-color Ramsey setting. This open problem, posed by the research group of Kuhn, Razanska, and Schlegel, asks for the ramsey top density of infinite trees and provides a lower bound of 3/4 based on an existing result by Erdos and Galvin. Since the conformal phase is inaccessible to direct computation owing to the model's analytic inaccuracy, its properties must be inferred indirectly. Quantum simulations employing cavity QED systems can provide an alternative route to examining the conformal phase, although the limited number fidelity of qudit preparation poses a constraint. This study utilizes qudits instead of qubits to overcome this fidelity issue, assessing various sound propagation properties in the conformal phase to verify the consistency of simulation results. Additionally, qudit quantization regulations are investigated to ensure the accessibility of simulation data. A proposed qudit duality technique is introduced to explore this issue further. Lastly, the potential of a specific, highly available qudit state preparation protocol is examined. This research paper focuses on two main concepts from geometry: Lie groupoids and stacks. Lie groupoids represent a non-abative generalization of Lie groups, while stacks can be viewed as non-abative versions of moduli spaces. Both of these concepts find applications across various fields, including physics, algebraic geometry, and topology. Within the framework of smooth spaces, we establish a universal geometric context where both groupoids and stacks can be defined. This universal context is made up of geometric configurations that are invariant under equivalence relations. By utilizing this universal context, we are able to generalize certain constructs, such as integrands and integrands on strata, from specific situations to more broad applications. Furthermore, we establish that both Lie groupoids and stacks can be constructed from geometric configurations, providing a direct relationship between these concepts and the initial space defined by equivalence relations. Additionally, we find that both groupoids and stacks possess natural properties when the space defined by equivalence relations satisfies specific conditions. These results also extend to the concept of presheaves. Moreover, we believe that this universal context may lead to new insights in fields such as algebraic geometry, topology, and theoretical physics. The connection between this context and Albin, Shmuelov, and Tolman's work on stack bundles is also worth noting. The paper also includes an appendix that provides an alternative interpretation of the concept of stacks as equivalence relations defined by geometric configuration equivalence. A key finding demonstrates that the one-step relation can be expressed in terms of the mean and covariance operator, effectively determining their distinguishing characteristics. Consequently, the study's results imply that the one-step relation's equivalence holds without any additional assumptions beyond its inherent properties. Furthermore, the study's framework is applied to investigate the fundamental properties of specific one-step relations, such as the L2 one-step relation, which leads to a more in-depth understanding of the sphere's geometric properties. A notable outcome of this investigation is the derivation of a formula for the L2 one-step relation's mean and covariance operator, consisting of a sum of the identity operator and the curvature tensor. This finding has implications for the study of stochastic fields on the sphere, offering a practical application of the one-step relation in the context of a stochastic field defined by its mean and covariance operator. Which in turn leads to an important discovery regarding the covariance operator's structure, specifically that it is directly linked to the geometric characteristics of the sphere. Complex liquid mixtures often exhibit varying levels of resistance to flow, a phenomenon that can be influenced by the interactions between different components and surface interactions with the container. In this study, we examine the surface tension and viscosity of bimodal liquid foams comprised of surfactant-free hydrocarbon liquids and a surfactant-based air phase, within a confined system subject to surface-interactive effects. By modulating the viscosity of the inner phase and the surface tension of the liquid-gas interface, we explore how viscosity and surface tension affect the flow resistance of bimodal liquid foams. Our results show that the viscosity of the liquid phase has a negligible impact on flow resistance, while surface tension exhibits a much greater influence. Furthermore, our data reveal a constant ratio existing between the surface tension and the square of the average bubble size, which in turn equals the ratio of the container's roughness to its radius. This ratio is independent of the distribution of viscosity and surface tension across different bubble sizes. Our research indicates that flow resistance in bimodal liquid foams is driven primarily by surface interactions and the ratio of the container's roughness to its radius, which in turn is determined by the ratio of the surface tension to the square of the average bubble size. This finding has implications for the behavior of complex liquids in confined systems and suggests that flow resistance could be an intrinsic property of the system, unaffected by the distribution of viscosity and surface tension across different bubble sizes. This is similar to the behavior observed in monodisperse liquid foams, where flow resistance is governed by the radius of the container and is independent of the distribution of viscosity and surface tension. Our results also demonstrate that flow resistance in bimodal liquid foams can be an intrinsic property of the system when the distribution of viscosity and surface tension across different bubble sizes is uniform. This is similar to the behavior observed in monodisperse liquid foams, where flow resistance is governed by the radius of the container and is independent of the distribution of viscosity and surface tension. To effectively train the model, a new learning objective is introduced that aligns the selected words with the target sentence, using a receptor network. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which outperforms conventional methods in various machine translation tasks. This results in the solitons and black holes being unique, with solutions being independent of the specific gauge group chosen. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. However, precise estimation of lateral displacement poses challenges due to noise and limited aperture size in ultrasound systems. To overcome this limitation, a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) algorithm is introduced to enhance the precision of elastography. In this approach, multiple scans are combined to create the illusion of a larger aperture with a virtual origin, and a sophisticated optimisation method is employed to determine the optimal scan configuration that maximises the precision of displacement estimation. The proposed VOSA algorithm is evaluated using phantom data and demonstrates superior performance in terms of displacement precision and noise resistance in comparison with existing elastography techniques. Furthermore, the efficacy of VOSA is demonstrated on a real-time elastography system for the diagnosis of breast tumours. The results indicate that the VOSA-based elastography technique outperforms the conventional technique by an overall precision of 62%, with a significant impact on the quantification of tissue displacement in the elastography system. The proposed VOSA algorithm has the potential to enhance the precision of elastography on a wide range of systems with varying aperture sizes. In a wide-ranging class of games, known as partial-information stochastic pursuit-withdrawal games, one player seeks to locate another who is moving randomly within a defined area. The relocating player can choose between continuing their search for a while or giving up the attempt. The game dynamics remain unchanged throughout the search. We have developed methods for dividing the game's territory into levels of varying difficulty, based on the probability of successful location. These hierarchical divisions vary with the speed and step length of the moving player. Our research shows that the most challenging regions are often situated near the perimeter of the search area. We have further found that the largest difficulty levels are stable and unaffected by changes in the moving player's speed and step length. This stability holds true as the speed and step length vary widely. We have also discovered that the most difficult regions usually contain the most valuable information about the moving player's location. This is especially true when the search area is large and the speed and step length of the moving player are low. Therefore, it is generally more beneficial for the relocating player to focus their search on these most difficult regions before giving up. We have developed various metrics to measure the difficulty of these regions and have found that the most challenging areas often exhibit complex behaviors that can be described as self-similar patterns. These patterns vary widely across different scales of measurement. This is especially true when the moving player's speed and step length fall within a certain range. When this condition is met, the probability distribution of the relocating player's successful location can be approximated as a beta distribution. This approximation holds true as the search continues and remains valid even after the moving player has been found. We have further investigated the effects of different speed and step length combinations on the difficulty levels and have found that the most challenging regions usually lie along the moving player's expected path. We have also found that the distribution of the difficulty levels can be influenced by changing the speed and step length of the moving player. This is often achieved by shifting the parameters of the beta distribution that models these difficulties. We have further developed methods for estimating these parameters from data obtained from partial-information stochastic pursuit-withdrawal games. These methods enable us to determine the probability distribution of the relocating player's successful location. This is true both when the search continues and after the moving player has been found. We have tested these methods on randomly generated games and have found that they accurately predict the probability distribution of the relocating player's successful location. This is true for a wide range of speed and step length

This research focuses on developing an efficient method for detecting vector bosons, specifically W and Z bosons, in high-energy muon collisions. Due to the vast amount of data involved, a fast vector boson estimation technique is crucial for historical muon data. To achieve this, we propose utilizing two approaches. First, we calculate the average transverse momentum of hadrons accompanying muons, which serves as a indicator of vector boson presence. To enhance accuracy, we also implement a machine learning model incorporating multiple features. This technique has been applied to both rapidity regions and produces reliable vector boson estimation. To further optimize the method for historical data analysis, we establish a relationship between the proposed estimation technique and the original variable, which in this case is the sum of the transverse energies of muons and hadrons. We also explore two variants of this approach for use in scenarios with limited data. To validate our method, we compare it to an alternative technique based on neural networks and find that it not only matches the performance of the rival method but also offers the benefit of being easier to implement. To facilitate analysis of vast amounts of historical muon data, we have developed a highly optimized version of this method that can be incorporated into existing data processing frameworks. To the best of our knowledge, this technique represents the most accurate neural network-based vector boson estimation model presented in the muon energy range in the scientific literature to date. This method has significant implications for ongoing and future experiments such as the Muon-to-GeV group at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider and the Muon Collusion at the Large Hadron Collider. To facilitate easy integration into these experiments, we have made our technique available as a standalone module that can be incorporated into existing data analysis frameworks. This approach has significant applications in scenarios with limited data and provides a promising foundation for the development of more advanced machine learning models that can be used in similar contexts. This research was conducted in partnership with the Muon-to-GeV group at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider.

The increasing complexity of real-world tasks means that agents must be capable of navigating multiple challenging tasks simultaneously. To prepare for such situations, an agent can benefit from interacting with highly intricate multi-task environments during the course of reinforcement learning training. However, experiencing significant difficulty in learning as a result of multiple overwhelming tasks can hinder an agent's progress, a problem we term 'catastrophic disruption.' In our research, we present a novel multi-task reinforcement learning system that is particularly effective in preventing catastrophic disruption, and our experiments demonstrate its superiority over multiple comparison methods in multiple complex multi-task scenarios. Furthermore, we discover that integrating a module-based system along with random task selection proves to be a highly effective method in preventing catastrophic disruption, a finding we believe can be a valuable guideline for future research. Our model-based method has also been successfully applied to challenging real-world problems, including multi-room navigation in the 'Gym MultiTask' domain and complex system control in the 'CartPole MultiTask' setting. Our approach, a modular version of the discrete action space algorithm, enables us to achieve a significant improvement in performance in comparison to multiple baseline methods in both scenarios. Our research can be expanded to incorporate multiple agent interactions in multi-task environments, and along with that, we present a novel multi-agent module-based system that is capable of interacting with a complex multi-task environment at the course of reinforcement learning training. Our experiments demonstrate that this system is highly resilient and able to adapt at a fast pace in comparison to multiple comparison methods in multiple complex multi-task scenarios. Our research can also be applied to simple multi-task scenarios, and in such cases, we find that our approach is capable of either matching or surpassing the performance of random task selection in a wide range of scenarios. Our research underpins a key premise that an agent should prioritize challenging tasks over effortless ones as part of its learning process, a concept we term 'task difficulty exploitation.' Our experiments demonstrate that integrating the principle of task difficulty exploitation into the reinforcement learning training process of an agent that is module-based proves to be highly effective in enhancing its performance in comparison to multiple comparison methods in multiple complex multi-task scenarios. We introduce a novel model where five specific types of digital trees gather under the direction of their individual natural numerals. Initially, each tree resides in a designated sector of a limitless, one-dimensional plane defined by the set of natural numbers. The plane's evolution is determined by simple rules: each tree moves horizontally or remains stationary based on a specific comparison with the numeral indicated at its leftmost edge; in response to this comparison, the tree then extends its edge horizontally or remains fixed. The rule that governs the tree's movement is aligned with the principles of intuitionistic logic. We prove that in this model, the trees that start in the leftmost sector will gather on the right, the trees in the sector numbered three will gather on the left, and the trees in the middle sector will disperse. Additionally, we provide explicit numerical boundaries for the gathering of the rightmost sector, the distance between the leading and trailing edges of the middle sector, and the location of the leading edge of the leftmost sector. In the process of our analysis, we introduce a new, intuitive metric that allows these conclusions to be drawn. Furthermore, we show that the rules governing the movement of the trees are equivalent to the application of the fixed point theorem as described by the Curry scheme, and that this situation can be extended to the movement of multiple trees. Lastly, we provide a precise numerical value for the distance between the leading and trailing edges of the leftmost sector, and offer a simpler, intuitive explanation for the behavior of the trees in this model. In the process of our analysis, we make use of a novel interpretation of the Godel operator that is motivated by the context of this model. This interpretation leads to the derivation of the Curry scheme by way of the fixed point theorem, and provides a reason for which intuitionistic logic is more conducive to gathering behavior than classical logic. In the course of our discussion, we also make reference to the original work of Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser, and offer a specific numerical value for the sum of the distances between the leading and trailing edges of the trees in the rightmost and leftmost sectors. Furthermore, we provide a general formula for the sum of the distances between the leading and trailing edges of the trees in any given sector, and offer a separate, independent proof for this formula based on the principles of classical logic. This latter proof leads to a different numerical value for the sum of the distances between the leading and trailing edges of the trees in the rightmost and leftmost sectors

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through diluted convolution layers. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an autoregressive approach with convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). However, its applications are restricted by its massive computational requirements and limited pitch control. To address these limitations, we introduced a DCNN-based pitch-related encoding framework for pitch-controlled WN, which produces high-fidelity audio via raw waveform generation. Comparative evaluations with WN and other baselines demonstrate the superior quality of QPNet-generated samples across various low-bitrate scenarios. Moreover, our findings indicate that the proposed framework automatically acquires the periodic characteristics of target signals, eliminating the need for input waveforms as guidance. Moreover, QPNet exhibits comparable performance to WN in tasks where pitch control is unnecessary, demonstrating its versatility. The code for QPNet is available at: https://github.com/Parandios/QPNet.

The bicategorical invariants theory has its foundations in the work of Vaishaw and Willmer, who generalized the Hermitian reciprocity law to the bicategorical framework. Building on this groundwork, we establish that shadows can be defined as bicategorical marks. This interpretation demonstrates that shadows possess properties analogous to Picard operators, which were initially observed by Jannsen in the context of cohomology. Additionally, it becomes apparent that the projection map from bicategorical marks to shadows acts as a factorization that incorporates the inclusion of shadows within Picard operators. Furthermore, it is shown that the projection map from bicategorical marks to shadows, when applied to a specific class of bicategorical marks, yields shadows that are equivalent to Picard operators, and this relationship can be expressed through the action of the Galois group. This equivalence is made explicit by means of a formula, which demonstrates the connection between the action of the Galois group on shadows and the operation of the trace map. This research was influenced by the results obtained by Jannsen in the context of cohomology, which can be viewed as a special case of bicategorical invariants theory. The development of bicategorical invariants theory also provides a framework for generalizing the properties of shadows, Picard operators, and Picard algebras that are derived from cohomology. The theory of bicategorical invariants can be applied to the Picard operators and Picard algebras that are derived from cohomology, which includes, for example, the algebra derived from the de Rham cohomology. The development of bicategorical invariants theory also enables the development of a framework for defining and studying the properties of shadows, Picard operators, and Picard algebras that are based on the cohomology of a group G, for any group G.
